articles.title: Lago formado após geleira ameaça provocar nova enchente no Nepal | G1
articles.standfirst: Reservatório pode se romper nos próximos três dias e já acumula cerca de 2 milhões de metros cúbicos de água, segundo o Times of India.
articles.summary: Reservatório já tem 2 milhões de metros cúbicos de água e pode receber outros 3 milhões nos próximos três dias, segundo autoridades chinesas
articles.body:
Um lago formado após o colapso de uma geleira na fronteira entre o Nepal e o Tibete, na China , pode se romper nos próximos três dias e provocar novas avalanches na região. O alerta foi divulgado pelo Times of India, com base em informações de autoridades chinesas.

O lago se formou perto da confluência dos rios Chhochen Khola e Purepu Tsangpo , no Nepal, segundo autoridades chinesas citadas pela imprensa estatal nesta quinta-feira (27).

O Ministério dos Recursos Hídricos da China informou que o reservatório acumulava cerca de 2 milhões de metros cúbicos de água (o equivalente a 800 piscinas olímpicas) até a manhã desta quinta e já estava transbordando.

A previsão é que outros 3 milhões de metros cúbicos de água cheguem ao lago nos próximos três dias. Com o aumento do volume, cresce o risco de rompimento da barreira natural, informou a emissora estatal CCTV.

As autoridades chinesas afirmaram que monitoram o lago continuamente. Também realizam simulações de possíveis enchentes e avaliações de risco para se preparar para um eventual rompimento e orientar as operações de resgate.

O alerta ocorre após o colapso de uma geleira no Tibete provocar uma série de enchentes e deslizamentos na região da fronteira entre China e Nepal.

Até esta quinta-feira, autoridades dos dois países informaram que mais de 300 pessoas morreram e cerca de 1.500 estão desaparecidas .

Os números ainda são provisórios e variam entre os órgãos responsáveis. As diferenças estão relacionadas aos métodos de coleta e verificação dos dados e às dificuldades de comunicação e coordenação nas áreas atingidas.

O possível rompimento do lago aumenta o risco para comunidades que já foram afetadas pela primeira enchente e pode dificultar ainda mais o trabalho das equipes de resgate.

articles.title: STJ começa a julgar pedido para que casal Nardoni volte à prisão | G1
articles.standfirst: Recurso apresentado por associação questiona cumprimento das regras do regime aberto pelos condenados pela morte de Isabella Nardoni em SP. Julgamento ocorre até 2 de setembro.
articles.summary: Recurso apresentado por associação questiona cumprimento das regras do regime aberto pelos condenados pela morte de Isabella Nardoni; julgamento ocorre até 2 de setembro.
articles.body:
O Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) começou a julgar nesta quinta-feira (27) um recurso que pede o retorno de Alexandre Nardoni e Anna Carolina Jatobá ao regime fechado. O mandado de segurança foi pedido pela Associação do Orgulho LGBTQIAPN+.

Condenados pelo assassinato de Isabella Nardoni, em 2008 , Alexandre e Anna Carolina atualmente cumprem pena em regime aberto. Eles sempre negaram o crime.

O recurso foi apresentado pela Associação do Orgulho LGBTQIAPN+, que alega que o ex-casal teria descumprido condições impostas pela Justiça para a manutenção do benefício da progressão de pena.

A análise ocorrerá de forma virtual na Quinta Turma da Corte e deve seguir até o dia 2 de setembro. O relator do caso é o ministro Ribeiro Dantas. Outros magistrados vão analisar o pedido.

O g1 procurou o STJ que confirmou a informação com a seguinte nota:

"O recurso está em julgamento no plenário virtual, mas como tramita em segredo de justiça, não temos mais informações a respeito até o momento. O julgamento começou à meia-noite de hoje (27) e vai até a meia-noite da próxima quarta-feira (2)."

A equipe de reportagem também tenta contato com a defesa do casal Nardoni.

Anna Carolina Jatobá (à esquerda) e Alexandre Nardoni (à direita) foram condenados pelo assassinato de Isabella Nardoni (ao centro) — Foto: Reprodução/Arquivo/TV Globo

"Informamos ao Superior Tribunal de Justiça que Alexandre e Jatobá estão descumprindo as medidas judiciais para ficar no regime aberto", disse Angelo Carbone, advogado da associação. "Ela também teve privilégios na cadeia enquanto esteve presa".

Segundo a entidade, Alexandre e Anna Carolina estariam circulando em horários supostamente incompatíveis com as regras do regime aberto, sem comprovar rotina de trabalho regular e com dúvidas sobre o endereço informado à Justiça.

A associação também afirma ter recebido relatos sobre a presença frequente de Nardoni e Jatobá em bairros da Zona Norte da capital paulista e em Barueri, na Grande São Paulo.

Alexandre Nardoni e Anna Carolina Jatobá, pai e madrasta de Isabella, sempre negaram o crime, mas foram condenados — Foto: Reprodução/Arquivo/TV Globo

"Foram mais de 2 mil pessoas que moram nessa região e que fizeram um abaixo-assinado pedindo a volta dos Nardoni para a cadeia", disse o advogado. "Essas assinaturas foram encaminhadas ao STJ".

Na manifestação anexada ao pedido, a associação afirma que o objetivo da ação não é questionar a condenação já definida pela Justiça, mas verificar se as condições para o cumprimento da pena em liberdade estão sendo respeitadas.

As defesas de Alexandre Nardoni e Anna Carolina Jatobá não haviam se manifestado sobre as acusações até a publicação da reportagem.

Alexandre Nardoni e Anna Carolina Jatobá foram condenados pela morte de Isabella Nardoni , de 5 anos, ocorrida em 29 de março de 2008. Segundo a acusação, a menina foi arremessada da janela do apartamento da família, no sexto andar de um edifício na Zona Norte de São Paulo.

O julgamento ocorreu em 2010. Nardoni, pai da criança, foi condenado a 31 anos de prisão por homicídio triplamente qualificado. Jatobá, madrasta de Isabella, recebeu pena de 26 anos de reclusão pelo mesmo crime.

Anna Carolina passou ao regime aberto em 2023 , após ter cumprido etapas anteriores da pena e obter progressões concedidas pela Justiça. Já Alexandre Nardoni deixou o regime semiaberto e passou ao aberto em 2024 .

A decisão da Quinta Turma do STJ poderá manter a situação atual dos dois ou determinar novo exame das alegações apresentadas pela associação sobre um eventual descumprimento das regras do regime aberto.

articles.title: Meta só pagará o valor integral de multa se YouTube e TikTok também fecharem acordo nos EUA; entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Dona de Instagram, Facebook e WhatsApp, fechou um acordo de US$ 18 bilhões com estados americanos para encerrar o processo que a acusa de incentivar a dependência de adolescentes das redes sociais.
articles.summary: Dona de Instagram, Facebook e WhatsApp, fechou um acordo de US$ 18 bilhões com estados americanos para encerrar o processo que a acusa de incentivar a dependência de adolescentes das redes sociais.
articles.body:
Segundo a Meta, o dinheiro deve ser usado para financiar atividades de segurança online para jovens e "outras prioridades estaduais".

O pagamento será dividido em duas partes. A primeira, equivalente a 70% do valor (cerca de US$ 12,7 bilhões ou R$ 65,6 bilhões), será feita em parcelas ao longo de 10 anos.

Os 30% restantes (cerca de US$5,3 bilhões ou R$ 27,4 bilhões) só serão liberados se duas condições forem cumpridas:

implementação de restrições para adolescentes no YouTube e TikTok, sendo elas o limite diário de uma hora de uso, modo noturno e medidas de verificação de idade;

YouTube e TikTok pagarem, cada um, um valor equivalente à parcela de 30%. A Meta exige que metade dos recursos restantes esteja vinculada ao pagamento do YouTube e a outra metade ao do TikTok.

Além do pagamento, a Meta também concordou em adotar novas regras para usuários menores de 18 anos que usam Facebook e Instagram nos Estados Unidos. As medidas deverão ser mantidas por 10 anos. Veja abaixo quais são.

Limite de tempo: adolescentes só poderão passar duas horas por dia no Facebook e no Instagram (o tempo de uso nas duas plataformas será somado). O limite só poderá ser desativado com autorização dos pais.

Modo noturno: os aplicativos serão bloqueados entre meia-noite e 6 horas da manhã.

Modo escolar: as notificações serão silenciadas por padrão entre 8 horas da manhã e 15 horas da tarde.

Lembretes regulares: adolescentes receberão avisos a cada 15 minutos de uso contínuo do Facebook e do Instagram. Também haverá lembretes aos 60 e 90 minutos de uso.

Controle do feed algorítmico: os usuários poderão optar por um feed sem personalização baseada no sistema de recomendações da Meta.

Controle de reprodução automática: a função poderá ser desativada.

Curtidas ocultas: adolescentes não verão, por padrão, o número de curtidas e reações nas publicações.

Desativação de filtros de cirurgia plástica e maquiagem extrema.

Verificação de idade: a Meta implementará medidas para identificar e remover crianças menores de 13 anos de suas plataformas.

Restrições de conteúdo adequado à idade: a empresa usará feedback e classificações de filmes para garantir que o conteúdo seja apropriado para cada faixa etária e impedirá que adolescentes sigam ou interajam com contas inadequadas.

Contato indesejado de estranhos: as contas serão definidas como privadas por padrão.

Denúncias e proteção contínua contra conteúdo prejudicial: : a Meta oferecerá mecanismos simples para denunciar conteúdos inadequados para adolescentes.

Fortalecimento dos controles parentais: a plataforma incentivará os pais a configurar ferramentas de supervisão.

O acordo encerra ações movidas por 29 estados americanos e põe fim a um julgamento federal considerado um dos principais testes, até agora, das acusações de que redes sociais prejudicam crianças e adolescentes, segundo a agência Reuters.

O julgamento começou em 12 de agosto e reunia ações judiciais iniciadas em 2023. Ao aceitar o acordo, a empresa de Mark Zuckerberg não admitiu ter cometido irregularidades.

O acordo também encerra processos movidos por Califórnia, Illinois, Novo México e Washington, D.C., relacionados ao escândalo Cambridge Analytica. O caso envolveu a coleta de dados pessoais de milhões de usuários do Facebook pela empresa de consultoria.

Esses estados receberão US$ 459,3 milhões para encerrar os processos.

Em um documento apresentado antes do julgamento, a Meta afirmou que os quatro estados buscavam multas de até US$ 1,4 trilhão.

Os estados não divulgaram um valor específico, mas disseram, antes do início do julgamento, que a quantia estaria mais próxima de US$ 200 bilhões. Também pediam indenizações adicionais e mudanças nas plataformas da Meta, incluindo medidas para impedir que crianças criassem contas.

Apesar do acordo, a Meta ainda enfrenta outras ações em tribunais federais e estaduais dos EUA, segundo a Reuters.

Nessas ações, a empresa é acusada de desenvolver deliberadamente recursos para aumentar o tempo que crianças e adolescentes passam nas plataformas, provocando dependência e contribuindo para problemas de saúde mental.

articles.title: Santo André e São Bernardo do Campo adotam medidas de prevenção de desastres para diminuir impactos do El Niño  | G1
articles.standfirst: Apesar das medidas, especialistas afirmam que os esforços feitos pelas prefeituras não são suficientes.
articles.summary: Apesar das medidas, especialistas afirmam que os esforços feitos pelas prefeituras não são suficientes.
articles.body:
Diante da possibilidade de eventos climáticos mais intensos por conta do El Niño, prefeituras de cidades da Grande São Paulo como Santo André e São Bernardo do Campo têm adotado medidas em diferentes frentes, como hidratação e proteção contra o calor, acolhimento da população vulnerável, monitoramento de áreas de risco, prevenção de desastres e medidas estruturais contra enchentes, queimadas e outros eventos extremos.

🔍O El Niño pode aumentar o calor e favorecer a ocorrência de temporais mais intensos na Região Metropolitana de São Paulo nos próximos meses. O fenômeno é caracterizado pelo aquecimento anormal das águas do Oceano Pacífico e provoca alterações nos padrões climáticos em diferentes partes do planeta.

Segundo o meteorologista César Soares, da Climatempo, o excesso de calor deve ser uma das principais características dos próximos meses no estado de São Paulo. As temperaturas elevadas também podem contribuir para a formação de nuvens maiores e núcleos de tempestade mais intensos.

"Mais calor traz o desenvolvimento de nuvens maiores e núcleos de tempestade mais intensos", explica o meteorologista.

A previsão é a de que os efeitos sejam mais sentidos no fim do ano e no começo de 2027, período em que podem ocorrer episódios de calor extremo e temporais na região.

Em Santo André, moradores de áreas consideradas vulneráveis participam de ações da Defesa Civil. É o caso da comunidade do Sítio Cassaquera, onde já foram registrados pelo menos dois deslizamentos de terra. O local também sofre com enchentes frequentes.

Em fevereiro de 2025, a água chegou à altura da canela de um morador em uma das vielas da comunidade. Em outra rua, carros tiveram dificuldade para atravessar o trecho alagado.

Enchente em viela de Santo André em 2025 — Foto: TV Globo / Reprodução

Para ajudar no monitoramento, moradores receberam capacitação do Núcleo de Proteção e Defesa Civil. Eles utilizam um grupo de comunicação para avisar sobre situações de risco, como deslizamentos, quedas de árvores e falta de energia.

Outra iniciativa envolve a instalação voluntária de equipamentos que medem o volume de chuva e a temperatura. Os moradores fazem o registro diário das informações, que são encaminhadas à Defesa Civil.

São Bernardo monitora 126 áreas de risco

El Niño aumenta preocupação em áreas que já sofrem com enchentes — Foto: TV Globo

Em São Bernardo do Campo, as ações são voltadas para prevenção e resposta a eventos como tempestades, temperaturas elevadas e ventos fortes.

A cidade possui 126 áreas de risco. Para acompanhar essas regiões, a Defesa Civil conta com mais de 40 pluviômetros, equipamentos que medem o volume de chuva, além de câmeras de monitoramento.

Segundo Marcos Cayres, coordenador da Defesa Civil de São Bernardo do Campo, a participação dos moradores é importante para identificar problemas e agir antes que ocorram situações mais graves.

"É fundamental que a gente possa conhecer onde estão os problemas, ter mapeado, e ter pessoas da sociedade civil preparadas para agir", afirma.

As medidas também incluem orientações para que a população se hidrate em períodos de calor e baixa umidade do ar.

Apesar das iniciativas adotadas pelas prefeituras, especialistas avaliam que as medidas emergenciais não são suficientes para enfrentar os impactos dos eventos climáticos extremos.

Para o SP1 , Pedro Torres, professor do Instituto de Biociências da Unesp, muitas das ações ainda são pontuais e reativas.

"Isso é necessário, mas não é suficiente", afirma.

Segundo o professor, medidas como a distribuição de água, acolhimento da população e mobilização da Defesa Civil deveriam fazer parte de uma política permanente de adaptação das cidades às mudanças climáticas.

Em nota, a Prefeitura de Santo André afirmou que mantém ações permanentes de prevenção e resposta a eventos climáticos extremos e que vem ampliando iniciativas de adaptação às mudanças do clima.

A Prefeitura de São Bernardo do Campo informou que possui um Centro Municipal de Emergências Climáticas e mantém o monitoramento das áreas de risco.

articles.title: After invasive rainbow trout threaten to erase Yellowstone’s native cutthroat fish, officials shut Buffalo Creek to wipe them out
articles.summary: US News: Yellowstone National Park is preparing to temporarily close part of Buffalo Creek as wildlife officials launch a targeted effort to remove invasive ra.
articles.body: Yellowstone National Park is preparing to temporarily close part of Buffalo Creek as wildlife officials launch a targeted effort to remove invasive rainbow trout threatening native fish populations. The conservation operation will begin on August 31, with the northern section of Buffalo Creek remaining closed to visitors until September 7 while biologists treat the waterway. According to NBC Montana, the park will use rotenone, an EPA-approved piscicide, to eliminate the invasive fish from the creek. Yellowstone National Park said the work is intended to protect Yellowstone cutthroat trout, the only trout species native to the park, from competition and hybridisation. The project forms part of a broader native fish conservation programme aimed at protecting the ecological health of the Lamar River watershed.Yellowstone closes Buffalo Creek for invasive trout removalBeginning August 31, Buffalo Creek will be temporarily closed from the northern Yellowstone boundary downstream to its confluence with Slough Creek. The closure is scheduled to last until September 7, allowing fisheries biologists to carry out the treatment without public access to the affected stretch. Yellowstone National Park said the operation will target invasive rainbow trout using rotenone, a piscicide approved by the US Environmental Protection Agency. The park has also confirmed that the treatment will not affect the potability of water at Slough Creek Campground, where drinking water will remain safe. Signs will be posted to alert visitors to the temporary restrictions. The announcement comes as Yellowstone continues efforts to prevent nonnative fish from spreading through sensitive waterways and undermining long-term native fish restoration projects.Invasive rainbow trout threaten Yellowstone cutthroat troutThe Buffalo Creek operation is focused on a population of invasive rainbow trout that has become a source of fish entering nearby waterways. According to Yellowstone National Park, these rainbow trout compete and hybridise with native Yellowstone cutthroat trout in Slough Creek, Soda Butte Creek and the Lamar River. This creates both ecological and genetic concerns because hybridisation can weaken the genetic integrity of native cutthroat populations. Yellowstone cutthroat trout are the only trout species native to the park and play an important ecological role across the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. The National Park Service says genetically pure populations have declined across their natural range because of competition, predation, hybridisation and habitat degradation. Removing the source population in Buffalo Creek is therefore considered crucial to maintaining the native trout population in the Lamar River watershed.Why Yellowstone uses rotenone to control invasive fishRotenone is not a new tool in Yellowstone's fight against nonnative fish. The National Park Service says piscicides such as rotenone are used because they can selectively target fish while conservation teams take steps to minimise impacts on other aquatic organisms. Before treatment, biologists survey the area and use the lowest effective concentration, while chemical use is timed to reduce risks to amphibians and other wildlife. Any native Yellowstone cutthroat trout captured through electrofishing before the Buffalo Creek project will be moved outside the treatment zone. Yellowstone has previously used rotenone during native fish restoration efforts, including projects in the Soda Butte Creek drainage. articles.body: American non-profit organisation, The Hindu American Foundation has issued an advisory ahead of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's event in New York City, advising citizens to stay vigilant, aware, and civilised."HAF is issuing this security alert in advance of the Universal Oneness Celebration at Madison Square Garden in New York City. Stay vigilant, remain situationally aware, and keep interactions civil. Ahead of the event, activists targeting Hindu Americans have attempted to disrupt and cancel the celebration", HAF posted on X, while also urging New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to ensure the safety of the event attendees.The community advisory was issued after intense criticism of the RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and his 'Universal Oneness Celebration', to be held on Saturday at Madison Square Garden.On Tuesday, Mamdani expressed his lack of support for Bhagwat's event while admitting his office cannot cancel it.“I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” he told reporters.United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) asked US government to consider sanctions against the RSS, alleging deterioration of religious freedom in India."We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat and making him ineligible for future entry into the United States", the body said.The USCIRF is Chaired by Pakistani-American Asif Mahmood.The body has previously been dismissed by the ministry of external affairs over bias and lack of credibility."We all know this is a biased institution. For years, it has made incorrect and provocative statements about India. We should ignore such institutions, as they have their own agendas and lack credibility", MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said during an August 21 press briefing.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1933, Herbert Hoover donated Rapidan Camp to the federal government for Shenandoah National Park; today, the former presidential retreat sits less than 90 miles from Washington, DC
articles.summary: US News: Discover the history of Rapidan Camp, the presidential retreat of Herbert Hoover, donated to the federal government in 1933 for Shenandoah National Park. Learn about its significance and preservation efforts today.
articles.body: In 1933, as Herbert Hoover left the White House after losing re-election, he donated Rapidan Camp, his secluded Virginia mountain retreat, to the federal government for incorporation into the future Shenandoah National Park. Today, the Rapidan Camp remains within the park, while the National Park Service describes Shenandoah as less than 90 miles southwest of Washington, DC. The former presidential retreat preserves the unusual setting where Hoover combined fishing and recreation with his federal work during some of the most difficult years of the Great Depression.A mountain retreat that became a presidential campPresident Hoover and his wife, Lou Henry Hoover, established Rapidan Camp in 1929, shortly after Herbert Hoover took office. The camp stood at the headwaters of the Rapidan River in the Blue Ridge Mountains and included several other rustic buildings surrounded by forest. While fishing was reportedly one of the president's favourite pastimes, the site was not simply a holiday retreat. According to the National Park Service, Hoover conducted official business there and held meetings with visitors, thus creating a working presidential camp far removed from the formal surroundings of Washington.The property covered about 164 acres and was privately owned by the Hoovers during his time as the country’s president. Furthermore, the location held significance as it was situated within the landscape being considered for the creation of Shenandoah National Park. The president supported the park project and intended to make the future park accessible. The camp consequently became a place where presidential recreation and government business overlapped. Hoover could fish in the surrounding streams and escape the capital’s political pressure while still receiving visitors and dealing with matters of state. The NPS describes the camp as Hoover’s “summer White House,” reflecting its role as a presidential retreat during his administration.Hoover donated the camp to the future parkHoover lost his 1932 re-election campaign to Franklin D. Roosevelt, whose inauguration took place in March 1933. As the former president prepared to leave office, he offered Rapidan Camp to the federal government for use as a part of the proposed Shenandoah National Park. The NPS timeline records the donation in 1933, thus allowing the camp to become a part of the federal park landscape that was being assembled in Virginia.However, Shenandoah was not yet a national park when Hoover made the gift. Congress had authorised the park in 1926, but Virginia still had to acquire and transfer the necessary land before the federal government could formally establish it. The park was eventually established on 26 December 1935, and Roosevelt formally dedicated the park on 3 July 1936.Roosevelt himself visited the Rapidan Camp on 9 April 1933, shortly after his inauguration, anchoring the transition between Hoover’s retreat and its eventual incorporation into Shenandoah. This specific visit allowed him to assess the property during the interim period between Hoover's donation and the land's eventual integration into the national park system. The landscape around the camp was also being transformed by the park’s development and by work associated with the Civilian Conservation Corps.A decade after the park's formal establishment, the Shenandoah superintendent reported in 1946 that the camp was sitting unused, and subsequently sought funding either to repair the buildings or demolish them. Instead, the property acquired a new use. In 1948, the Boy Scouts of America received a 20-year lease to use the camp as a summer facility, a decision consistent with Hoover’s wishes for the property.Further rehabilitation took place between 1960 and 1963, and decades later the NPS carried out a restoration focused on historical accuracy. After decades of exposure had led to the dismantling of the site's temporary structures, in 2004, the agency completed the restoration of the grounds and the three surviving cabins associated with Hoover’s retreat: the Brown House, Prime Minister’s Cabin and the Creel Cabin. The agency’s work aimed to preserve the appearance and character of the camp during the Hoover years instead of leaving the buildings to deteriorate.Therefore, the preservation of Rapidan Camp offers a link to a pivotal era in American history. The historic cabins that would have otherwise deteriorated now stand as an educational resource in Shenandoah National Park, thus allowing modern visitors to explore the unique environment where a president found solace during the heights of the Great Depression.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump’s ‘unique’ diplomacy gives hope to families detained in China
articles.summary: Grace Jin Drexel was living in agony for seven months, advocating for the release of her father from a Chinese prison, when a friend mentioned to her in early May that her phone must be blowing up. A short time earlier, President Trump, in response to a question from The Hill, had said he would…
articles.body:
Grace Jin Drexel was living in agony for seven months, advocating for the release of her father from a Chinese prison, when a friend mentioned to her in early May that her phone must be blowing up.

A short time earlier, President Trump, in response to a question from The Hill, had said he would raise the issue of Ezra Jin, the leader of the Zion Church in China who was arrested in October, when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in October.

“Huge, huge!” Drexel told The Hill in an interview in Washington about the moment that changed everything in the effort to secure her father’s release. She was holding her 2-month-old son, Ezra, who is named for her father.

Shortly after she saw Trump answer The Hill, Drexel during an interview with Fox News thanked the president. It’s an appearance she believes furthered efforts to win the pastor’s release.

Jin was freed in July, two months after Trump met with Xi in Beijing and personally raised the issue of releasing the church leader.

The whole episode served as a somewhat textbook case of how to appeal to Trump for results: Raise an issue personally with the president, reinforce it on Fox News and show him he could yield tangible wins.

Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit in Washington on Sept. 24, Drexel believes the time is now to ask the president to advocate for the release of at least eight Zion Church leaders still detained in China on religious freedom grounds.

“From my perspective, why not ask for the stars? If not me, who is going to be asking? There are so many people still detained in China,” she said.

A White House official told The Hill that Trump is “always concerned about Americans detained abroad” when asked whether they expect the issue will come up during Xi’s visit.

“As he has said publicly, President Trump raised Pastor Jin’s detention directly with Xi Jinping. He will always champion religious freedom around the world,” the official said.

It’s not clear if that formula can be repeated next month.

Both leaders are keen on improving the relationship between the world’s two largest economies.

The leaders are expected to grapple with the issues of trade policy, artificial intelligence regulation and the Iran and Ukraine wars.

Trump has put China in the crosshairs of his new economic pressure campaign against Iran, telling Beijing to cut financial ties with Tehran or risk punishing U.S. sanctions.

“We’re really grateful for what he did and showed us that our nation is great in taking care of and becoming a voice of the voiceless in this way,” she said.

Trump had also raised Youlin Chen, a Chinese-born American seismologist who has been in a Chinese jail since 2024. The U.S. designated Chen as “wrongfully detained” in March but kept his case quiet, hoping behind-the-scenes advocacy would be more successful than a public naming-and-shaming campaign.

When Trump left China without Chen, the administration and Chen’s family went public in July, hoping the attention would increase pressure on Xi.

There’s little indication that Xi is bending, however. Instead, he has been jailing more Americans.

In June, American academic Min Zin was arrested while traveling to China to attend a conference. The administration has labeled him as “wrongfully detained.”

Still, families of other prisoners in China have taken note of Trump’s personal involvement in Jin’s release.

“It just shows that sustained advocacy at a high level, it does work and diplomacy does work,” said Rayhan Asat, a Uyghur human rights lawyer whose brother is currently detained in China.

Trump, during his first term, determined the Chinese Communist Party was committing genocide in Xinjiang against its population of Uyghur Muslims and other ethnic groups, saying the campaign stretched to 2017.

Asat’s brother, Ekpar, disappeared 10 years ago upon returning to Xinjiang from a trip to Washington, D.C., following participation in the State Department’s International Visitor Leadership Program. Outspoken critics of the Chinese government often find their families targets in China, or themselves the victims of harassment — wherever they live — as part of China’s transnational repression efforts .

Asat has since met with officials at the State Department and White House, including in the second Trump administration, to advocate for her brother’s release.

“I’m very optimistic that my brother would be released,” Asat told The Hill. “But for that to happen President Trump needs to keep raising cases so we don’t lose momentum.”

A number of detained Chinese citizens have family members who are American citizens.

Dr. Gulshan Abbas, whose sister is Uyghur American activist Rushan Abbas, has been imprisoned in China since 2018. Gulshan Abbas vanished from her hometown of Urumqi, the capital of the Uyghur Autonomous Region, days after Rushan Abbas criticized the Chinese government’s treatment of the ethnic group during remarks at the Hudson Institute in Washington.

That type of transnational repression is a shared experience among families of loved ones detained in China.

Drexel said she and her U.S.-based mother have experienced harassment and surveillance.

In one chilling episode, her mother picked up a phishing phone call that transferred her to a police station in China. She’s had her tires slashed in a private garage, and Drexel said she’s observed people filming her.

Drexel quit her job as a Republican national security staffer on Capitol Hill to advocate for her father’s release full time.

“In a sense, that’s China’s long-arm in another way,” she said of leaving her job.

“When a family member has someone detained in China, there’s enormous pressure because you feel like you’re going against the whole state apparatus, which in this case, it was, the whole state apparatus is out to get you.”

Sarah Makin, who served as senior director on the National Security Council during Trump’s first term and works with the Abbas family and others who have loved ones imprisoned in China, said Trump’s positive relationship with Xi works in their favor.

“The way that he has handled that relationship, has set us up for success here, and has set him up for success in getting as many people out as possible,” Makin said.

“On these cases in particular, this is the thing I’m focused on when it comes to China, and I think he’s the best guy for the job right now,” she added.

Still, she argued advocates for those imprisoned need to continuously put pressure on those around the president to help move the needle.

“Whether that’s people who have the president’s ear or groups or communities that he really listens to for moral guidance and clarity, we’ve got to get them to recognize how the [Chinese Communist Party] in this case is using these cases and these prisoners to hurt the American people,” Makin said.

Advocates say that if Xi fails to answer U.S. demands, Trump could take a number of actions to raise the pressure.

This includes raising the travel advisory against China from a Level 2 to a Level 3, which would urge Americans to reconsider travel. Advocates say adding a disclaimer that China is known to arbitrarily detain U.S. nationals adds even more pressure — causing businesses and academics to reconsider investment and travel in China and increasing insurance costs.

“Those things do have serious implications,” said Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer of the nonprofit Global Reach, which helps advocate for Americans unjustly detained and is working on Youlin Chen’s case.

A “nuclear option” is to label China a State Sponsor of Wrongful Detention, a new label created by Congress to deter U.S. hostage taking.

The Chinese came out against the U.S. creating that label at the time, when Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian was asked whether China could be targeted, and he rejected that it detains people for political purposes.

“When the U.S. designates somebody [as wrongfully detained], that never goes away. It’s going to be on the agenda of every senior leader engagement until it’s resolved,” Lebson said.

“I think there’s a lot of positives that the Chinese want from the U.S. or the U.S. wants from China, and hopefully the Chinese will see that … resolving it would be a gesture of goodwill to a president who has made it a hallmark of his second term to focus on bringing home Americans.”

articles.title: Dominican Republic joins global fight against antisemitism with landmark move
articles.summary: Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun called the Dominican Republic's IHRA adoption a "historic moment" and urged other Latin American governments to follow suit.
articles.body: The Dominican Republic is set to become the 48th country in the world and the seventh in Latin America to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism after President Luis Abinader ordered the country’s foreign ministry to formalize the decision. The move came as Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun, the U.S. special envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism, urged other Latin American governments to follow the Dominican Republic’s lead, pointing to the Trump administration’s efforts at home as a framework for confronting antisemitism internationally. Abinader made the announcement Monday at the Combat Antisemitism Movement-sponsored annual Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism in the nation's capital, Santo Domingo. According to an English translation of the president’s remarks, Abinader said antisemitism should not be viewed as a threat affecting only Jewish communities. "Antisemitism is not a problem that concerns only the Jewish people," he said. "It is a threat to democratic coexistence and to the rights and freedoms of us all." A NEW CHAPTER FOR AMERICA’S 250TH: 'J250' INITIATIVE PUTS JEWISH CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE SPOTLIGHT The announcement comes amid heightened concern over antisemitism worldwide. The Combat Antisemitism Movement’s Antisemitism Research Center monitored and reported 767 antisemitic incidents globally in March 2026, an average of nearly 25 incidents per day and a 32.5% increase compared with March 2025. Kaploun praised the Dominican Republic’s decision at the conference as a "historic moment" and called on other governments across the region to follow its lead. "What you have witnessed tonight is a government standing up for what is right," he said. "There cannot be any compromise with antisemitism," he continued. "We will lead by example, and we will take positive steps to protect every Jewish community." Kaploun pointed to the Trump administration’s efforts in the United States as a framework other governments could use to confront antisemitism within their own institutions. 'NOT ON OUR WATCH': GLOBAL LAW ENFORCEMENT LEADERS UNITE IN POLAND AGAINST HATE "In America, we have our marching orders," he said. "We are holding universities accountable. We are prosecuting hate crimes. We have changed our visa vetting programs. We have withdrawn from major U.N. bodies that have promoted terrorism and antisemitism." The U.S. State Department has used a working definition of antisemitism, together with guiding examples, since 2010. In 2016, the IHRA’s member countries adopted the current non-legally binding working definition. The IHRA describes antisemitism as "a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred toward Jews." It further explains that antisemitism can include rhetorical or physical manifestations directed against Jewish or non-Jewish individuals, their property, Jewish community institutions or religious facilities. Its non-legally binding definition and accompanying examples are intended to help governments, law enforcement agencies, universities and other institutions identify contemporary manifestations of antisemitism and respond to incidents more consistently. CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM The accompanying examples address conduct including Holocaust denial, conspiracy theories about Jewish power, holding Jewish people collectively responsible for Israel’s actions and applying standards to Israel that are not demanded of other democratic nations. As of the end of 2025, 1,334 governments, public institutions, universities, nonprofit organizations, corporations and sports organizations worldwide had adopted or endorsed the IHRA definition, according to data compiled by the Combat Antisemitism Movement’s Antisemitism Research Center. Abinader told the conference that, "Rejecting antisemitism does not mean taking a position regarding a particular government or conflict," he added. "It means stating unequivocally that no political disagreement, no cause and no circumstance can justify hatred, discrimination, or violence against an individual or a community." Abinader said the definition would provide the country with a framework for identifying and combating different forms of antisemitism while respecting freedom of expression and other rights protected by the Dominican Constitution. CRITICS SAY TURKEY'S VERBAL ATTACKS ON ISRAEL HAVE CROSSED INTO ANTISEMITISM "Through this decision, the Dominican Republic reaffirms its commitment to the memory of the Holocaust, to the protection of Jewish communities and to the eradication of antisemitism in all its forms," he said. "Human dignity is indivisible and its defense admits no exceptions." The president connected the decision to the Dominican Republic’s history of offering refuge to Jews fleeing Nazi persecution. Following the 1938 Évian Conference, hundreds of Jewish refugees established a community in Sosúa, where they were able to rebuild their lives. Abinader also announced that his government would commit 50 million Dominican pesos toward constructing a new building for the Jewish Museum of Sosúa to preserve that history. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Once the Foreign Ministry formalizes the decision, the Dominican Republic will join Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Panama and Uruguay as the Latin American countries that have embraced the IHRA framework. The decision adds to growing regional acceptance of the definition and could set a precedent for additional Latin American governments considering how to formally identify and address antisemitism. Abinader concluded his remarks with a call for the region to act: "From this land, which at different moments in its history has offered refuge and hope, let us send a firm message throughout Latin America and the Caribbean: Indifference must never prevail in the face of hatred." "May this forum enable us to turn memory into education; education into prevention; and our principles into concrete action," he added. articles.title: Ex-waitress reveals restaurant tipping secret most customers don't realize — expert calls it 'bad hospitality'
articles.summary: A mentor at the Red Rooster Tavern taught Mel Robbins which diners actually influence the tip, sparking debate among hospitality and etiquette experts.
articles.body: Mel Robbins learned an unusual lesson about earning big tips when she worked as a waitress: Pay attention to the women at the table. The bestselling author and podcast host recently recalled advice from a "mentor-boss" at the Red Rooster Tavern in Michigan about figuring out who really influences the gratuity. "She told me when I started waitressing the secret to getting a good tip: Understanding who has influence over who gives you the good tip," Robbins told The Wall Street Journal. SHAKE SHACK CUSTOMER HITS 'NO TIP' AT KIOSK, THEN WATCHES PRICES JUMP IN VIRAL VIDEO Most might assume that if a man picks up the check, he's also deciding the tip. But Robbins said her mentor taught her otherwise. "What happens when the check comes and you've had a really good server? What happens often is the women turn to their partners and say, 'She was great. Give her a good tip,'" Robbins recalled, adding that she learned "to ignore the men and to completely take fabulous care of the women." Robbins may be onto something about the social dynamics surrounding a tip — although hospitality and etiquette experts caution against ignoring anyone at the table. "I don't entirely disagree," Robert Mahon, managing partner of New York-based Mahon Hospitality Group, told Fox News Digital. "In my experience, when a man is paying, the woman will often have the final judgment on the service and may suggest the tip." AUTOMATIC TIP OR SERVICE CHARGE? NEW STATE LAW REQUIRES RESTAURANTS TO TELL DINERS BEFORE THEY ORDER But, he added, focusing solely on the women and ignoring the men is "just bad hospitality." "We would never encourage a server to show favoritism," Mahon said. Instead, Mahon said skilled servers pay attention to the dynamics of the entire group. "The best servers read the whole table," Mahon said. "Regardless of gender, people naturally respond to someone who is friendly and engaging. Ultimately, big tips come from making everyone at the table feel well-looked-after." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Research suggests there is more psychology behind a generous tip than simply providing good service. In one experiment, communication researchers John S. Seiter and Harry Weger Jr. examined whether something as simple as complimenting customers could affect gratuities. Four restaurant servers waited on 360 dining parties, either complimenting diners on their food selections or refraining from doing so, according to a study published in 2010. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The researchers found servers received significantly higher tips when they complimented diners — evidence that small interpersonal interactions can potentially influence what customers leave behind. Lisa Burdette, founder of the Dallas School of Etiquette, told Fox News Digital it's true that women can have an influence over a man's tip. But, she said, "a good server should always concentrate on all customers, never slighting anyone." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Etiquette dictates that the person picking up the check ultimately determines the gratuity, Burdette said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It should never be a topic of debate at the table," she said.

articles.title: Could UK military sites come under attack? London gets warning from Russia
articles.summary: International News: Vladimir Putin-led Russia on Thursday warned that it could strike British military targets “inside and outside Ukraine” in a response to Ukrainian att.
articles.body: Vladimir Putin-led Russia on Thursday warned that it could strike British military targets “inside and outside Ukraine” in a response to Ukrainian attacks using British-supplied missiles.The warning came from Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s visit to Kyiv, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Ukraine’s Independence Day.Zakharova urged Britain to back away from what she called London’s hostile approach towards Russia, warning that it risked taking the conflict to an “entirely new level”.Speaking at a briefing in Moscow, she also accused Britain and France of “playing with fire” by supplying sensitive missile technology to Ukraine.Earlier, security sources cited by the Daily Mail warned that Russia could mount a “direct response” against Britain amid concerns in Whitehall that Moscow may have underestimated Burnham’s commitment to Ukraine.The warning follows Britain’s decision to provide Ukraine with blueprints for British-made components used in the Storm Shadow cruise missile, allowing Kyiv to produce the long-range weapon domestically.Moscow reacted angrily to the move, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying on Monday that Britain’s involvement was preventing “even the slightest progress” towards peace.Britain announced on Monday that it would grant Kyiv access to classified technology to begin domestic production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles, capable of striking deep inside Russia. France has also agreed to license the technology for the European missile.

articles.summary: Nchimbi announced his resignation earlier this week after reportedly falling out with President Samia.
articles.body:
Emmanuel Nchimbi has been expelled from Tanzania's ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party for indiscipline following his decision earlier this week to resign as the country's vice-president after 10 months in the job.

The 54-year-old has made some controversial remarks in recent weeks - including urging Tanzanians to "fight for a new constitution" - pointing to a possible fallout with President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

He was Samia's running mate in last October's disputed presidential election, which saw hundreds killed in post-poll unrest.

Energy Minister Deogratius Ndejembi, 43, has been nominated as his replacement and his name will now be presented to parliament for approval.

The decisions were taken at an extraordinary meeting of the CCM, chaired by President Samia.

The party did not give details about the indiscipline allegations against Nchimbi, whose resignation takes effect at the end of next week.

Nchimbi, who shared his brief resignation letter on his Instagram account on Tuesday morning, is the first vice-president to step down in Tanzania's history.

He said he would retire from public life as he had "become convinced, without doubt, that the president wants changes".

Samia and Nchimbi were sworn in last November after winning 98% of the vote.

The election was boycotted by the main opposition party, Chadema, which had called for electoral reforms as a precondition to taking part.

Violent protests in the awake of voting led to the deaths of at least 500 people, according to an official enquiry.

Opposition parties and human rights groups accused the security forces of unleashing a brutal crackdown on anti-government protesters.

articles.title: Massachusetts police officer resigns hours before termination hearing after allegedly using Flock and police databases to track former partner; town removed its last Flock camera
articles.summary: US News: A police officer in the small Massachusetts town of Stow has resigned just hours before a scheduled termination hearing, after an internal investigati.
articles.body: A police officer in the small Massachusetts town of Stow has resigned just hours before a scheduled termination hearing, after an internal investigation found he repeatedly misused surveillance tools to track a former partner. Officer Jason Rogers allegedly used Flock Safety’s automated license plate reader system and state police databases to obtain information about the woman with no legitimate law enforcement purpose, according to town officials and police statements. In response, Stow cancelled its contract with Flock Safety and removed the town’s last Flock camera in early August, according to NBC Boston's report and official statements from the Stow Police Department. Here's what actually happened:Allegations surface after victim files complaintStow police said they first learned of the allegations on June 18, when the victim filed a formal complaint with the department. Officials did not initially disclose the exact nature of Rogers’ relationship with the victim, but local reporting and court documents indicate she was a former romantic partner.Within hours of receiving the complaint, the department placed Rogers on paid administrative leave and revoked his access to all internal systems. The swift action reflected the seriousness of the allegations: misuse of law enforcement databases is not only a policy violation, but a potential crime.What the internal investigation foundOver the next four weeks, the Stow Police Department conducted an internal affairs investigation into Rogers’ use of department resources. Investigators concluded that he had: Illegally accessed Criminal Offender Record Information (CORI) through the Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) system on at least five separate occasions; and used the Flock Safety automated license plate reader system and CJIS to run vehicle information on multiple dates, without any legitimate law enforcement reason.The department said its findings sustained multiple charges against Rogers, including conduct unbecoming an officer, improper use of an official position, failure to comply with written orders, use of false and unsubstantiated search reasons, and violations of department policies governing law enforcement databases.From administrative leave to criminal chargesInitially, the Stow Select Board scheduled an employment status hearing for Rogers on July 30 to determine his future with the department. That hearing was postponed, and the town placed Rogers on unpaid administrative leave the following day. A new hearing was set for August 26.After receiving the internal affairs report, Stow police opened a separate criminal investigation. As a result, they filed a criminal complaint seeking charges against Rogers for alleged illegal use of the CORI system. The case has been forwarded to the Middlesex District Attorney’s Office for prosecution.In addition, the internal affairs report was sent to the Massachusetts Peace Officer Standards and Training (POST) Commission. The POST Commission has the authority to decertify officers, which would bar Rogers from working as a police officer anywhere in the state.Resignation before hearingHours before the August 26 termination hearing, Rogers resigned from the Stow Police Department, according to town officials. His resignation ends the employment proceedings but does not affect the criminal case or the POST Commission’s review of his certification.Town ends relationship with Flock SafetyIn a significant policy move, Stow police said they have terminated their relationship with Flock Safety as a direct result of Rogers’ actions. In early August, the department removed the last Flock automated license plate reader camera it operated in town.Flock Safety’s system uses high-resolution cameras and artificial intelligence to read license plates and cross-reference them with databases, helping police track stolen vehicles, locate suspects and find missing persons. But the technology also creates a detailed record of where vehicles travel, raising concerns when it is misused for personal reasons.Stow Police Chief Michael Sallese said the department will present an updated policy for automated license plate readers to the Select Board at a later date, aiming to strengthen oversight and prevent similar abuses in the future.“A serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime”In a public statement, Chief Sallese emphasised the gravity of the situation. “Law enforcement officers are entrusted with access to sensitive information solely so they can perform their official duties and protect the public...Using that access for a personal purpose is a serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime,” he said.Sallese added that the department acted quickly to remove Rogers from duty and protect its systems once the complaint was received. “We conducted a thorough investigation and are pursuing both employment and criminal accountability,” he said.Town Administrator Denise Dembkoski echoed that message, stressing that Rogers’ alleged conduct does not reflect the values of the department as a whole, according to NBC Boston. “The actions of one individual do not represent the values or conduct we expect from the good and dedicated members of the Stow Police Department,” she said, as per the report.Dembkoski praised the department’s leadership for responding “immediately” and following the evidence to produce a comprehensive internal affairs report. “We will continue working to ensure that the public has confidence in how sensitive law enforcement information is accessed and protected,” she added.Part of a broader pattern in MassachusettsThe Stow case emerged just days after a similar scandal in New Bedford, where police paused their use of Flock Safety cameras after an officer was accused of using the system to track a former girlfriend’s vehicle. That case, first reported by the New Bedford Light, has prompted calls for stricter oversight of automated license plate readers across the state.More than 100 communities in Massachusetts currently use Flock technology, according to local reporting. As these tools become more widespread, the potential for misuse, especially in cases involving domestic violence, stalking or personal disputes, has become a growing concern for privacy advocates and lawmakers.Flock responds with new safeguardsIn response to mounting scrutiny, Flock Safety’s CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, announced that the company is updating its privacy and security standards. Among the changes is a mandate that all customers adopt a feature that flags abnormal activity in audit logs, which track every search and query made in the system.“We knew that abuse was a risk nine years ago, which is why we mandated that every customer had to have an audit log,” Langley said in a video statement. “We are finding bad cops and holding them accountable.”The company says it is working to improve detection of potential misuse and to support agencies in enforcing strict use policies.What comes next for Stow and its residentsFor the victim in the Stow case, the outcome of the criminal and certification proceedings will be closely watched, according to the report. She has said she changed her identity after leaving an abusive relationship, only to discover that Rogers had allegedly used police tools to track her movements.For the town, the focus now shifts to rebuilding public trust and ensuring that powerful surveillance technologies are used only for legitimate law enforcement purposes, with robust oversight and accountability. As Stow drafts its updated automated license plate reader policy, the Rogers case is likely to serve as a cautionary example of what can happen when those safeguards fail.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Researchers examined pilot whales stranded around Hawaii over 13 years; 3 had swallowed up to 12 pounds of marine debris, including as many as 35,543 pieces of plastic in a single stomach
articles.summary: US News: Massive tangles of discarded fishing lines, ropes and plastic bags are harming marine life in the Pacific, with deep-diving whales swallowing thousand.
articles.body: Massive tangles of discarded fishing lines, ropes and plastic bags are harming marine life in the Pacific, with deep-diving whales swallowing thousands of plastic pieces in Hawaiian waters. A 13-year study of stranded short-finned pilot whales around the main Hawaiian Islands found that nearly 23 per cent of the animals examined had swallowed synthetic waste. Researchers at the Health and Stranding Lab at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa found that three adult males had each swallowed up to 12 pounds (5.4 kilograms) of ocean debris. The findings, published in the scientific journal Marine Pollution Bulletin, offer detailed evidence of how plastic pollution is entering the digestive systems of deep-sea predators. Full necropsies of the three whales revealed huge amounts of synthetic waste packed inside their stomachs. Tests showed that the whales had swallowed between 6,283 and 35,543 separate pieces of plastic larger than 5 millimetres, about the width of a standard pencil eraser.“The presence of human-made materials in the stomachs of these ocean sentinels serves as a stark reminder of the impact of global plastic pollution,” said Kristi West, director of the UH Health and Stranding Lab and corresponding author on the study. “It is a clear message of the importance of keeping these materials out of our ocean.”Fishing waste is the biggest threatMost of the waste found inside the whales came from abandoned, lost or discarded fishing gear, often known as ghost gear. Strong monofilament fishing lines, synthetic ropes and pieces of fishing nets made up most of the material recovered from the animals. The second-largest group was flexible plastic sheets, including carrier bags, household rubbish sacks and industrial packaging. Although small pieces were much more common, larger objects accounted for most of the total weight. Items longer than 200 millimetres, or about 8 inches, made up more than 70 per cent of the total weight of the plastic recovered from the three whales.Deep-sea hunting increases the riskShort-finned pilot whales (Globicephala macrorhynchus) are large marine mammals found in tropical and warm temperate oceans around the world. They are capable of deep dives and can travel hundreds of metres below the surface while hunting prey with echolocation. Researchers said the whales may be especially vulnerable to plastic because of their diet. Pilot whales mainly eat squid, which can move and feel similar to floating plastic sheets, submerged bags and fishing lines drifting through the water. The location of the Hawaiian Islands may also increase the danger. The islands are downwind and downstream from the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a large area of floating marine waste northeast of Hawaii. Ocean currents can carry fishing gear and other plastic waste towards Hawaiian waters, where pilot whales feed.Plastic can cause long-term harmDespite carrying large amounts of plastic, all three adult males were in normal physical condition before they stranded. Researchers did not identify the debris as the main or immediate cause of death. However, scientists warned that this does not mean the whales were unharmed. Large amounts of plastic can take up valuable space in the stomach, leaving less room for food and potentially causing long-term nutritional stress. Over time, this could weaken the immune system of marine mammals. Plastic can also create chemical risks. Synthetic materials in the ocean can absorb pollutants, including polychlorinated biphenyls and heavy metals, and can release chemicals from the plastic itself. As plastic breaks down inside an animal, some of these substances can enter surrounding tissues and build up in organs and blubber, potentially affecting health and reproduction.Years of researchThe study's findings came from more than seven years of field collection, laboratory work and tissue preparation. A team of 25 researchers, graduate students and field technicians helped recover the stranded whales, carry out necropsies and sort thousands of pieces of plastic. The project received financial support from the Environmental Readiness Division of the Commander, United States Pacific Fleet, as well as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Fisheries John H. Prescott Marine Mammal Rescue Assistance Grant programme. Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi said stranded whales can provide important information about the health of remote marine ecosystems that are otherwise difficult to study. The large amounts of plastic found in Hawaiian pilot whales underline the need for stronger international action on discarded fishing gear and single-use plastics before pollution causes further damage to marine food webs.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Harry and Meghan arrive for ‘extended’ stay in the U.K. six years after royal exit
articles.summary: Prince Harry and Meghan arrived back in the U.K.  after six years in California, a source close to the family confirmed to NBC News.
articles.body: LONDON — Prince Harry and his family sought to begin a new life for a second time as they arrived back in the United Kingdom on Wednesday after six years in California, a source close to them confirmed to NBC News. The Duke of Sussex, 41, and his wife, Meghan, 45, flew in on a private plane with their two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, according to several media reports. A spokesperson for the Sussexes declined to comment on where the family would be living, citing privacy and security concerns. However, the spokesperson did confirm that they brought their dogs with them, although their chickens would remain in Montecito, California, where the family had been living since 2020. A source close to the couple told NBC News last week that they were moving back for an “extended period” of time. Harry and Meghan rattled the British royal family six years ago when they opted to step down as working royals, eventually choosing a quieter life in the affluent coastal enclave in Santa Barbara. Relations have been strained in the years since, worsened in part by explosive allegations of racism and bullying made by the couple in their Netflix documentary “Harry & Meghan” and in Harry’s memoir, “Spare.” After years with few signs of a royal rapprochement, Britain was shocked last week when it emerged they were planning a return. Harry and Meghan will remain private individuals and nonworking members of the royal family, a source familiar with the couple’s plans told NBC News last week, while reports in British media indicated that Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in schools in the country. Questions remain over what security arrangements will be in place for the couple, after a protracted legal battle between Harry and the British government over the removal of their security protection. Asked about their security last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “This is a private matter, it’s a matter for Harry and Meghan, and we wish them well in the moves that they’re making.” The couple’s planned return had sparked a slew of media coverage, with front pages dominated by unconfirmed reports that Meghan could return to acting for the first time since she departed the television show “Suits” ahead of her 2018 wedding to Harry. Harry’s return to Britain also comes after he and several other claimants were ordered to pay a combined £34.5 million ($46 million) to a major newspaper publisher after losing a High Court battle over alleged breaches of privacy. That battle was one of several salvos between Harry and the British press.

articles.title: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's US event organiser AHEAD’s X account restored after brief suspension
articles.summary: US News: The X account of AHEAD, the organiser of RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's upcoming event at Madison Square Garden, was briefly suspended before being restored. The organisation alleged that opponents tried to manipulate the platform to block their account. Amidst controversy over the event, security advisories have been issued for attendees.
articles.body: The X (formerly Twitter) account of American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD), which is organising Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat’s event at New York’s Madison Square Garden, has been restored after a brief suspension. AHEAD said it believes opponents used automated activity to get the account blocked and thanked X for restoring it.“We are back up! We got ‘botted’ by misguided opponents who tried to game the X algorithm and get our handle blocked. A big thank you to @X @Support for the prompt response, restoring our account and clearing out the bots. Now, back to what really matters: celebrating Universal Harmony and Universal Oneness @Uni1ness,” AHEAD said in a post on X.The account, operating under the handle @AheadForum1, had earlier become unavailable to users on Thursday. AHEAD had initially said it believed the suspension may have occurred in error.Bhagwat is scheduled to address the “Universal Oneness Celebration” at the Infosys Theatre at Madison Square Garden on August 29. The programme is expected to draw around 5,000 Indian Americans as part of the RSS's global outreach during its centenary yearEarlier this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he did not support the planned event, while acknowledging that his office may not have the authority to cancel a private gathering.“I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani told reporters on Tuesday.Mamdani's comments have triggered criticism among sections of the Indian-American diaspora and have also drawn opposing reactions from Indian political parties. His remarks came as left-liberal groups criticised the event and called for its cancellation.The controversy has also prompted a security advisory from the Hindu American Foundation (HAF), a US-based non-profit organisation. HAF urged people attending the event to remain vigilant, stay aware of their surroundings and keep interactions civil.HAF said the advisory followed attempts by activists targeting Hindu Americans to disrupt and cancel the celebration.It also called on Mamdani to ensure the safety of people attending the event.The event has also drawn scrutiny from the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), which has urged the US government to consider sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials it alleges are involved in religious freedom violations in India.“We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat and making him ineligible for future entry into the United States,” the body said.The commission is chaired by Pakistani-American Asif Mahmood.India's Ministry of External Affairs has previously rejected USCIRF's assessments, accusing the body of bias and questioning its credibility. During an August 21 press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the commission had made what he described as “incorrect and provocative statements about India” for years.“We all know this is a biased institution. For years, it has made incorrect and provocative statements about India. We should ignore such institutions, as they have their own agendas and lack credibility,” Jaiswal said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Russia warns it could target UK in response to Kyiv firing British missiles
articles.summary: Foreign ministry warns against ‘terrorism’ of firing long-range British cruise missiles at targets in Russia.
articles.body:
Moscow has warned that it could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine if Kyiv continues to fire long-range UK-made cruise missiles into Russia.

The warning, delivered by Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova at a news briefing in Moscow on Thursday, is the strongest direct threat yet to Britain, a key NATO member and ally of Ukraine.

Zakharova said London was “one step away” from becoming legally complicit in what she described as “terrorism” against Russian civilians, warning of “catastrophic consequences” unless Britain changed course.

“We have repeatedly warned that any British military installations and equipment in Ukraine and beyond its borders could be targeted in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory carried out using British weapons,” she said.

“We propose that the British leadership once again carefully analyse the situation and immediately, in the most resolute and unequivocal manner, abandon the hostile, aggressive line,” she added.

The warning came a day after Moscow accused Ukraine of firing British Storm Shadow missiles to attack a shopping centre in the Russian-controlled city of Donetsk, an attack Russian officials said wounded civilians, including children.

The Kremlin previously accused Britain of adding “fuel to the fire” after London announced it would allow Kyiv access to technology to build Storm Shadow cruise missiles locally. France has already agreed to license the technology for the European missile.

The diplomatic warning coincides with a new wave of Russian missile and drone attacks across Ukraine, targeting key infrastructure and leaving at least one person dead and several injured.

“Overnight, Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukraine, targeting ports, grain storage, energy, industry and other infrastructure with ballistic and hypersonic missiles and combat drones,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.

The Ukrainian air force said air defences downed seven ballistic missiles, one anti-ship cruise missile and nearly 90 percent of the incoming drones.

In Kharkiv, one person was killed and two were injured in a lunchtime attack on a shopping centre, according to regional governor Oleh Syniehubov.

Falling debris in Kyiv damaged a school, shattered windows at a healthcare facility and wounded two people outside the capital. Attacks on industrial and energy sites in the Poltava region cut power to seven settlements.

Steelworks and industrial facilities were struck in Kryvyi Rih and Zaporizhzhia, injuring six people in both cities. In Odesa, three people were injured in an hours-long attack which damaged port infrastructure, an educational facility and a multi-storey building.

Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed it targeted steelworks in Kryvyi Rih and Zaporizhzhia, an oil refinery in Poltava, logistics hubs near Kyiv and three ports in Odesa.

In central Russia, the online retailer Ozon said a drone attack damaged a logistics complex in the latest in a series of strikes on its facilities.

articles.title: Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic dies
articles.summary: The ‘butcher of Bosnia’ died age 84 in a UN prison hospital in the Netherlands, the UN tribunal in The Hague confirmed.
articles.body:
⁠Former Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic, ⁠who was ⁠serving a life sentence for ‌genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the bloody 1992-1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has ⁠died.

Mladic, 84, the so-called “butcher of Bosnia”, died at a United Nations prison hospital in the Netherlands, the UN tribunal in The Hague confirmed on Thursday.

“Mladic passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague,” said the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, adding that judge Graciela Gatti Santana had ordered “a full inquiry into the circumstances” of his death.

A family member of Mladic confirmed the reports of his death earlier in the day and told The Associated Press that Mladic’s son, Darko Mladic, was on his way to The Hague.

Mladic was convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 massacre of at least ‌8,000 Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) boys and men in a UN-designated “safe area” of Bosnia, in Europe’s worst atrocity since World War II.

He spent his last years in jail after he was convicted in 2017 for crimes the tribunal said at the time were “amongst the most heinous known to humankind”.

Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein described him as “the epitome of evil” after his conviction.

The former communist officer-turned nationalist warlord was one of the most notorious figures of the conflict in which more than 100,000 people were killed and more than two million were driven from their homes.

He commanded his troops to “scorch the brains” of the Bosniaks and boasted of being a “Serbian god”.

When the Bosnian war started in 1992, Mladic became the commander of the Bosnian Serb troops and took control of large swaths of the country in an attempt to form a Serb mini-state.

Serbs under Mladic’s control laid siege to the capital, Sarajevo, and other cities and villages, established camps for detained Bosniaks and enemy soldiers, and systematically killed prisoners.

The killings, recognised as a genocide, were the culmination of a war that had ⁠lasted at least three years, in which Mladic pounded Sarajevo daily with the artillery, tanks, mortars and heavy machineguns of his nationalist Serb army, killing 10,000 people.

The dead from Srebrenica were bulldozed into mass graves over four days in July 1995, some of them dug up and relocated to remote mountains in order to hide evidence of the killings.

The goal, as determined by the UN International Criminal Tribunal for the ⁠former Yugoslavia (ICTY), was “ethnic cleansing” — the forcible expulsion of Bosniaks, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian lands for a Greater Serbia.

The tribunal found that Mladic, together with late Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadzic, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.

Defiant to the end, Mladic said, “I do not recognise this court,” at an ICTY hearing of his case in 2014.

When he was sentenced to life in prison ⁠in 2017 he shouted: “This is all lies, you are all liars!”

Mladic death ‘doesn’t clear the mass graves’

Despite Mladic’s crimes, many Serbs continue to revere a military commander who painted himself as a “simple man” whom fate had chosen to protect his people.

Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik reacted to Mladic’s death saying: “It is a murder. He was respected by Serbian people. As a commander ‌he stood to defend Serbs.”

Remir Suljagic, the head of the Srebrenica memorial, however said it is important to remember Mladic’s victims and not glorify him after his death.

“It doesn’t bring back the dead. It doesn’t clear mass graves. It does not ‌change judgments. It does not turn the criminal into a historical figure.” Suljagic said.

Kada Hotic’s husband and son were killed by Serb forces in 1995. They were 56 and 29 at the time.

The 82-year-old told Reuters that justice has been served because Mladic died in prison. “I am grateful to the Tribunal because it sentenced ⁠Mladic to life and has not released him. He died ⁠in disgrace, because he killed so many people.”
