articles.title: Bipartisan lawmakers turn up pressure on Serbian president as elections loom
articles.summary: A pair of bipartisan lawmakers is sending a warning to Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić to answer anti-corruption demands and sever ties with America’s adversaries or risk sanctions from the U.S. Reps. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) and Bill Keating (D-Mass.), members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced legislation Thursday calling for sanctions and visa bans on…
articles.body:
A pair of bipartisan lawmakers is sending a warning to Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić to answer anti-corruption demands and sever ties with America’s adversaries or risk sanctions from the U.S.

Reps. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) and Bill Keating (D-Mass.), members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced legislation Thursday calling for sanctions and visa bans on individuals who undermine democratic processes, peace, stability and territorial integrity in the Western Balkans.

The bipartisan broadside against Vučić stands in sharp contrast to the generally warm relationship the longtime Serbian leader has shared with President Trump.

Trump counts his 2020 effort to normalize ties between Serbia and Kosovo as one of the major peace efforts he’s taken on while in office — integral to his image as a “president of peace.” And Vučić, speaking to Breitbart News in May , sent out a public appeal to Trump by touting that Serbs overwhelmingly support the U.S. president.

But Wilson and Keating’s legislation serves as a message of solidarity with student-led, anti-corruption protests that have plagued the Serbian leader for two years. The protests were triggered by a railway station tragedy in November 2024 where 16 people died after a canopy collapsed.

The demonstrators argue the railway station disaster was a symptom of broader government mismanagement of construction projects and corruption.

“Under President Vucic, Serbia has deliberately drifted further from Rule of Law and nearer to enemies of freedom like War Criminal Putin, the Chinese Communist Party, and the terrorist regime in Tehran,” Wilson said in a statement to The Hill, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Despite widespread protest of corruption, the Vucic government threatens to destabilize the region and beyond. The people of Serbia deserve better,” the South Carolina Republican added.

Keating also noted that the legislation makes clear Vučić and other Serbian government officials must make progress on anti-corruption efforts and combat influence from Iran, Russia and China.

“Democracy, rule of law, and anti-corruption must remain key pillars in the U.S.-Serbia bilateral relationship,” he said.

The bill text directly calls out Vučić for using excessive force against the protesters , demands an investigation and accountability into the railway tragedy and raises concerns over Serbia’s deepening ties with Iran, Russia and China.

“The United States has an enduring interest in a stable, democratic, and sovereign Serbia that is committed to regional peace and security and firmly anchored in Euro-Atlantic institutions and free from malign external influence,” the bill text reads.

Vučić, who has held power as president and prime minister for 12 years, announced in late July he would resign within weeks, and that new parliamentary and presidential elections would take place on Oct. 18 or 25.

But there’s concern over whether those elections would be free and fair, or whether the leader would use them to reinforce his control. Freedom House rates Serbia as “partly free,” noting that over the course of 2025, Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party “has steadily eroded political rights and civil liberties, putting legal and extralegal pressure on independent media, the political opposition, and civil society organizations.”

Trump last spoke with his Serbian counterpart by phone shortly after winning the 2024 presidential election , but the two men have not appeared to meet face-to-face since 2020. Still, Vučić hosted the president’s son, Donald Trump Jr., twice in Belgrade this year . And in July, the U.S. and Serbia hosted their first “strategic dialogue,” viewed as a significant elevation of Belgrade’s relationship with Washington.

Wilson and Keating address the strategic dialogue in their legislation, calling for the secretary of State to raise four key issues with Belgrade: Serbia’s relations with Russia, China and Iran; ensuring free and fair elections in Serbia; anti-corruption, public procurement, and rule of law reform in Serbia; and strengthening democratic governance, the freedom of the press, and freedom of assembly in the Balkan country.

If the secretary fails to provide the certification to Congress, the legislation demands the administration end the strategic dialogue or cut any funding related to the dialogue.

articles.title: Trump administration won’t ‘just sit down and take’ further retaliation from Canada: Trade rep
articles.summary: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Wednesday said the Trump administration would not “just sit down and take” further retaliation from Canada after Ottawa introduced a dollar-for-dollar match on U.S. tariffs. “If there’s further retaliation from the Canadian side, we, of course, we’re not going to just sit down and take that. Our view is…
articles.body:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Wednesday said the Trump administration would not “just sit down and take” further retaliation from Canada after Ottawa introduced a dollar-for-dollar match on U.S. tariffs.

“If there’s further retaliation from the Canadian side, we, of course, we’re not going to just sit down and take that. Our view is don’t retaliate,” Greer said during an appearance on CBC’s “The National.”

“But I know that, you know, I know how people are feeling in Canada and what they think. So, you know, it’s unfortunate, but it is what it is. And we have our own trade policy, and we’ll proceed with it in the way that’s best for the United States,” he added.

President Trump introduced a 50 percent tariff on around $20 billion worth of Canadian goods on Sunday after attempting to negotiate an agreement that the U.S.’s northern neighbor ultimately backed out of .

Greer said Canada asked for some concessions that were considered “too much.”

“It wasn’t something we could do at the time,” he said Wednesday. “We felt that giving them the best deal in the world would have been enough to get us over the hump and put us on a positive track to even bigger and better things.”

Instead of acquiescing to the deal, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with retaliatory import taxes that are set to go into effect on Sept. 8 .

The trade representative also acknowledged that the only other country to push back on tariffs with its own measures was China.

“Canada is the only country to retaliate against us besides China. And even with China, we’ve kind of settled out. So really, it’s just Canada at this point,” Greer said.

“We think they need to do more to protect the North American market,” he added.

The president has emphasized his goal of boosting domestic manufacturing and has pressured American companies not to outsource jobs and production by imposing sweeping tariffs on a long list of foreign trading partners.

The effort hit a roadblock earlier this year after the Supreme Court struck down the bulk of his emergency levies, but the administration has turned to other measures to implement import taxes.

articles.title: Ratko Mladić, Bosnian-Serb general dubbed the ‘Butcher of Bosnia,’ dies aged 84
articles.summary: Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb general who orchestrated the Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo during the Balkan wars, has died
articles.body: Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian-Serb general who orchestrated the Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo during the Balkan wars, has died in prison aged 84. Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia,” Mladić was convicted in 2017 by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) for masterminding a campaign of ethnic cleansing against Bosnia’s non-Serb population in the early 1990s. The UN-established court found him guilty of genocide, crimes against humanity, persecution, extermination, murder, terror, unlawful attacks on civilians and hostage-taking. At the time of Mladić’s indictment, ICTY Judge Fouad Riad described the actions the former general oversaw as “unimaginable savagery.” Mladić died while serving a life sentence at the UN Detention Unit in The Hague, his lawyer Dragan Ivetić told CNN. He spent just over 15 years in prison. Following his conviction, Mladić made multiple appeals and requests for release on medical grounds. The last of these was filed by his lawyers just last week. They asked for an early release on humanitarian grounds, quoting the detention unit’s doctors as saying that his “overall condition has rapidly declined” and warning that his death “may occur at any time.” The request was denied. ‘Scenes from hell’ Mladić was born on March 12, 1942, in the municipality of Kalinovik in what was then Yugoslavia. Born at the height of World War II, his early life was deeply affected by the conflict – his father Nedja Mladić was killed by the Ustasha regime, a Croatian fascist movement which was installed by the Nazis and Fascist Italy in occupied Yugoslavia, and which perpetrated genocide against Jews, Serbs and Roma. Ratko Mladić trained at the military academy of the Yugoslav People’s Army in Belgrade. He graduated in 1965, joined the Communist Party and became a career soldier. After the breakup of Yugoslavia, Mladić became the Commander of the General Staff of the Army of the breakaway Serb Republic in Bosnia, which was backed and armed by the Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic. As the army chief, Mladić was the main architect of a brutal campaign of ethnic cleansing, directly overseeing widespread and indiscriminate killing, deportations and forcible transfers of civilians. While Mladić was found guilty of a number of atrocities, two of his crimes have become synonymous with the terror he inflicted on the Muslim and Croat population of Bosnia during the war: the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica massacre. Under his command, Bosnian Serb forces besieged the city of Sarajevo from higher ground in 1992. They trapped its residents in the valley below for two years, conducting frequent shelling and sniper attacks against the civilian population. More than 10,000 people, including many children, died during the siege. In July 1995, Mladić spearheaded an attack on the Muslim enclave of Srebrenica, which was designated a “safe place” by the UN. The massacre remains Europe’s worst atrocity since World War II: More than 7,000 Muslims, mostly men and boys were slaughtered within a few days. Riad described the events that took place in Srebrenica as “truly scenes from hell, written on the darkest pages of human history.” “Thousands of men executed and buried in mass graves, hundreds of men buried alive, men and women mutilated and slaughtered, children killed before their mothers’ eyes, a grandfather forced to eat the liver of his own grandson,” the judge said as Mladic’s indictment was announced. Years on the run While Mladic was indicted by the ICTY in November 1995, he managed to evade justice for 16 long years. He first took refuge in Belgrade, living under Milosevic’s protection. When the former Serbian president was arrested in 2001, Mladić went into hiding, eluding authorities for another decade. He was finally captured in Serbia in May 2011 and was extradited to the Hague shortly after that. His trial lasted more than four years and was, in many ways, the culmination of the work of the ICTY. It was the tribunal’s last major case, and it included harrowing testimonies from hundreds of witnesses. Mladic showed little remorse during the proceedings and denied any responsibility. He blamed the actions he was being tried for on subordinates who executed his orders. In his closing argument, ICTY prosecutor Alan Tieger had described Mladić as “the master of life and death.” “The time has come for General Mladic to be held accountable for those crimes against each of his victims and the communities he destroyed,” Tieger said. “No one can fathom the extent of the sufferings for which Ratko Mladic is responsible.” This story has been updated.

articles.title: The new sanctions bill is aimed at the wrong Russia
articles.summary: While the Senate passed the Graham sanctions package to penalize Russia’s war economy, critics argue that true peace requires explicitly weakening Moscow’s military capacity through direct support for Ukraine’s defense.
articles.body:
The Senate passed the Graham sanctions package 86-11 this month, the most substantial move this year to shift the dynamic of Russia’s war on Ukraine.

Should it pass the House, the bill will give the Trump administration sharper tools to penalize countries that keep buying Russian oil and gas, to target the shadow fleet of reflagged tankers and hit Russian banks and energy projects. “Today we say to Vladimir Putin: You will not conquer Ukraine,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said from the Senate floor.

Economic pressure can make a real difference. But sanctions are a means to an end, and Washington has yet to articulate it. Words like “settlement,” “peace deal” and even “with Ukraine as long as it takes” leave the central questions unanswered: How do we break Moscow’s appetite for war-making? Why is Putin refusing to quit a campaign of terror? How many elderly Ukrainians must Russian troops hunt in the streets with killer drones, in what has been termed a human safari , before America recalls what it promised Ukraine in the Budapest Memorandum ?

The theory of halting Russian aggression buried inside the bill goes like this: drain the revenue, raise the cost, let the pain accumulate until Moscow decides the war is no longer worth it. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) said the pressure will push Putin to revisit peace negotiations seriously.

We know that the Kremlin doesn’t answer to the people it governs, but the bill’s logic naively assumes it cares for them. Moscow has spent five centuries proving otherwise. Under tsars, commissars and now kleptocrats, the Kremlin has readily sacrificed the lives of Russians to preserve its grip on its colonial possessions from Kamchatka to Kaliningrad.

In July alone, Russia suffered an estimated 42,860 soldiers killed or wounded , nearly twice as many casualties in one month as the U.S. military sustained over two decades of war in Afghanistan. Total Russian casualties may now be approaching 1.5 million.

Surely, our lawmakers are thinking, there must come a point when too many men have died, too much treasure has been wasted for too little gain, and Moscow grows desperate to sue for peace.

And this is their faulty assumption. The Kremlin is pushing in the exact opposite direction from what conventional logic would dictate. Having rejected every overture since March of last year, when Ukraine promptly agreed to the unconditional ceasefire the Trump administration put on the table, Moscow also scoffed at a limited Black Sea truce suggested by Ankara just this month.

America’s foreign policy has for decades been calibrated to a Russia that does not exist. Our collective imagination still conjures a nation with national interests, but the Frankenstein polity stretching across 11 time zones is decidedly not that. Lenin called the tsarist realm a “prison of nations” in 1914, and so Russia remains a century later.

The Russian Federation is an empire in the most literal sense — a predatory leviathan built on subjugation, extraction and dispossession. The Kremlin loots oil from Siberia, diamonds from Sakha and conscripts soldiers from dozens of subjugated nations, feeding the colonized into the furnace of yet another colonial conquest.

The Financial Times reported in February that men from Buryatia and Tuva were 25 times more likely to perish in Ukraine than men from Moscow. Michael Kofman of the Carnegie Endowment observed that Moscow had built a pipeline for assault troops and “largely didn’t care about expending these people.”

Sanctions restrict Moscow’s cash flow and, if effectively enforced, could make its war-crimes machine sputter. But using pain to coax the Kremlin toward negotiations is a fool’s errand — and so is waiting for the Russian people to grow tired of war. Rather, the strategic purpose of economic pressure must be to weaken and ultimately remove Moscow’s capacity to wage war.

The U.S. must therefore be explicit about the outcome that will give peace a chance. That means supplying Ukraine with the long-range weapons needed to destroy enemy missile production sites and military airfields. The shadow fleet is not something for America to name and shame; sanctioned vessels should be boarded and seized.

Starving Moscow of energy revenues and investing heavily in Ukraine’s defense industry are obvious next steps. Peace secured by leaving Russia capable of another war will lead, at best, to an intermission. But if history taught us anything, it’s more of a red carpet for World War III.

Article Five has been invoked only once in NATO’s history, in defense of the U.S. after 9/11. Washington should consider what its European allies would expect if the next test came in reverse. What if Romania had failed to intercept an explosive-laden Russian naval drone in the Black Sea? What if the drone that U.S. intelligence linked to Moscow at a German airport had struck its intended target? If one of these provocations crosses the line, the White House will face a choice between abandoning the alliance and entering a war with Russia.

Unpunished evil spreads and grows; every high schooler knows that. Does Washington? American security and credibility will not be restored while, for 12 long years, Russia is given a free hand to wage its horrific, terrible war; while it supplies the ayatollahs in Iran with intelligence to target U.S. forces.

A recent Pew Research Center poll finds that two-thirds of Americans lack confidence in President Trump’s handling of Russia’s war. Only 20 percent say Ukraine is receiving too much support, and 83 percent view Russia unfavorably. With the midterms approaching, it is a small wonder that lawmakers are eager to pass the Graham Act . But sanctions accomplish little without a clear purpose. That purpose must be to render Moscow’s grievance-fueled predation impotent.

Andrew Chakhoyan is an academic director at the University of Amsterdam. He previously served in the U.S. government at the Millennium Challenge Corporation and studied at Harvard Kennedy School and Donetsk State Tech University.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods leave hundreds missing, including 65 Americans
articles.summary: A New York couple traveling to Mount Kailash is among 65 Americans missing after a catastrophic flood along the Nepal-Tibet border.
articles.body: The last time Radhika Sharma heard from her parents, they had just crossed from Nepal into Tibet. Ramesh Sharma, 65, and Neelam Sharma, 64, who live in New York and are U.S. citizens, were making a religious pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a peak in Tibet considered sacred by Hindus, Buddhists and other faiths. Shortly after their border crossing Wednesday, a towering torrent of water, rock and mud tore through the same Himalayan corridor. Videos from the hardest-hit border regions showed people running as the debris flow swallowed buildings and vehicles, devastated towns and settlements, and severed roads, power and communications. The suspected collapse of a melting glacier shook the ground so violently that seismic monitors initially registered it as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake. In one video from Mailung, in Nepal’s Rasuwa region, a group of construction workers were seen walking down a mountain path before noticing giant plumes of brown debris in the distance, rapidly cascading toward them. The men reversed course to flee uphill, one briefly stopping to film before realizing the scale of the danger. He shouts in Nepali: “Oh, my God, the flood is getting so big! Let’s run — run fast, guys! Oh, my God, get back quickly!” By Thursday afternoon, authorities had recovered 289 bodies in Nepal and confirmed three deaths in Tibet. Hundreds more remained unaccounted for. Nepal’s Tourism Board said 644 travelers, including 65 Americans, were missing. Sharma’s parents were among a group of seven people making the journey to Mount Kailash, visited by tens of thousands of pilgrims each year. “It has probably been the worst 24 hours of my life,” Sharma, a doctor, 32, based in North Carolina, said in an interview with NBC News as she continued an anxious wait for news. The hardest part, she said, was the not knowing. She has contacted the U.S. embassies in Nepal and China, as well as American officials domestically. “I haven’t heard anything back”, she said. After posting pleas on social media, she has been put in contact with people in Nepal “who are trying to help track down my parents,” she said. “I’ve given them my parents’ information, their photos. I’m on the phone now, just waiting to hear someone say that they’ve even seen them.” Sharma is far from alone in desperately seeking information about loved ones. The State Department said in a statement Wednesday that it was “working closely with local authorities to locate and assist U.S. citizens in the affected areas,” telling concerned relatives to contact its emergency line. Even before the disaster, this was a remote, mountainous area where travel and communication were difficult. The flood then destroyed roads and knocked out power and phone networks, leaving families unable to establish even the most basic facts. In Baidur, Nepal, Shova Shrestha, 33, has spent more than a day waiting for news of her missing husband, Rajan Shrestha, as rescue efforts continue. “I keep looking at each helicopter, hoping he will step out of it,” she told The Associated Press. Sagar Pandey, chief executive of the tour company escorting travelers from Australia, India, the U.S., Canada and Singapore, could only assess the devastation where they had been from a helicopter. “There are no human-made things, no human settlement left. Everything is just flat,” he told Reuters. “So anyone in the hotel, the restaurant or the car, I believe that everybody is gone.” Syed Sadique, who runs a tour agency based in southern India, was waiting anxiously for news on the fate of 57 people traveling with his company, including his tour guide son, Sayed Umar Farook. “The group ⁠was traveling on three buses in Nepal,” he told Reuters. “A member of the group told us that one vehicle carrying about 20 people managed to get through safely, while passengers saw another bus plunge ​into a gorge.” Amid the carnage and chaos, and her desperate outreach to authorities and locals, Sharma sent a message to her missing parents themselves. She said she told them: “I love you. I am looking for you. I will keep looking for you. I just hope you’re OK.” Sharma added: “I know that wherever they are, they’re probably a lot more worried about my brother and I, because that’s just the type of people they are.”

articles.title: Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić dies aged 84
articles.summary: He was jailed for life in 2017 for genocide, war crimes and crimes against  humanity during the wars in the ex-Yugoslavia in 1992-95.
articles.body:
Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić has died in a UN prison at The Hague aged 84.

He was jailed for life in 2017 for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the wars in the former Yugoslavia in 1992-95.

After the Bosnian war, he went on the run for 16 years until he was finally tracked down in rural Serbia in 2011 and put on trial in the Dutch city.

The sentence for the man known as the "Butcher of Bosnia" was upheld on appeal by the UN court in 2021. He was being given palliative care in the hospital of the UN detention facility, where he died.

In a statement confirming the death on Thursday, the UN Court said Dutch authorities have begun an investigation.

It added that the court's top judge"has ordered a full inquiry into the circumstances" of Mladić's death.

In May, the court rejected a bid for his release from jail as he was nearing the end of his life.

The judge agreed his situation was "dire" but ruled that he was receiving "comprehensive and compassionate treatment" in prison.

Mladić's lawyers said at the time that he had already been bedbound or in a wheelchair for a long time and later had suffered a suspected stroke that left him almost unable to speak.

Mladić - who never recognised the UN court - had been held at The Hague detention facility since 2011.

He commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.

During the war his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the main city of Sarajevo with the deaths of more than 10,000 people, and carried out the massacre of 8,000 men and boys at Srebrenica.

Hasan Hasanović , a Srebrenica survivor who lost his twin brother and father in the massacre, told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme that Mladić's death "does not bring closure because the people who were killed in Srebrenica cannot come back".

"His death is just a biological necessity, and it doesn't bring to an end the political project and military project that created that legacy of genocide. And we now live with the consequences of a divided country, genocide denial," said Hasanović, who now works at the Srebrenica memorial centre.

However, Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik told Reuters news agency that Mladić "was respected by Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs."

In Serbia's capital Belgrade, some local residents also praised him.

"I genuinely believe he protected the Serbian people, because after all, that was his duty," a man called Milan was quoted as saying by Reuters.

Another man, Vasilije, said: "It's a massive shame, it really is. Personally, I think it's a total injustice that he was even thrown in The Hague."

articles.title: Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions
articles.summary: Nickolay Mladenov warns that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.
articles.body:
A senior official on US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.

Nickolay Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.

He was speaking to the UN Security Council after Israel rejected the 15-point roadmap for Hamas's disarmament, which was announced by the Board of Peace last month.

Hamas has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal. But Israel has insisted that the group must fully disarm before any pullout.

At least 1,303 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks in Gaza over the same period.

Israeli attacks kill five in Gaza, including two children, medics say

UK, Canada and Australia condemn Israel for refusing criminal probe into aid worker killings in Gaza

Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza

The Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza told the Security Council on Wednesday that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed at their last meeting on a mechanism through which his government's remaining questions would be settled and that committees had been established for that purpose.

Mladenov said that process had not stalled but warned that risks remained, including the continued killing of Palestinian civilians in Israeli strikes.

"A ceasefire in fact under which civilians are still buried is not yet one that the people of Gaza can really feel. Every use of force that does not answer an immediate threat, and every incident that the deconfliction mechanism was not asked to resolve, costs this process something very hard to buy back," he added.

Mladenov acknowledged that Hamas too had yet to meet fully its commitment to cease all military activities.

"Every weapon carried, every tunnel still worked and every convoy still obstructed sets the process back and hands an argument to those who want to resume war," he said.

He repeated that under the new roadmap, Israeli troop withdrawal from Gaza "follows verified decommissioning" of Hamas weapons handed over to the Palestinian technocratic committee that will govern Gaza under the Board of Peace's supervision.

"It is sequenced and reciprocal," he said.

That is a key difference from comments made by President Trump's envoy, Jared Kushner, after meeting Israel's prime minister two weeks ago.

He said Israeli withdrawal would be discussed only once the demilitarisation of Gaza was "done" - appearing to change the plan in line with Israel's demands.

Israel's representative told the Security Council meeting that it was committed to last October's US-brokered plan for ending the Gaza war, but she insisted it could not succeed while Hamas still had weapons, tunnels and other military infrastructure.

"Disarmament must come first," she stated.

The Palestinian representative said Israel was killing Palestinian civilians with impunity in Gaza and called on the international community to protect them without delay.

Mladenov warned that if the ceasefire was allowed to collapse, "there will be no roadmap to return to, there will be no administration to deploy, and there will be nothing left of the ground to rebuild".

"That would not be a setback. It would be a point of no return for everyone."

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,430 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

articles.title: CIA director warned Russia against attacking NATO: Reports
articles.summary: A surprise visit to Moscow by the head of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) served to warn Russia against launching an attack against NATO countries, according to multiple reports. President Trump described CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s trip as “semi-routine” in an interview on Wednesday, and Baltic officials — on the border with Russia and its…
articles.body:
A surprise visit to Moscow by the head of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) served to warn Russia against launching an attack against NATO countries, according to multiple reports.

President Trump described CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s trip as “semi-routine” in an interview on Wednesday, and Baltic officials — on the border with Russia and its ally Belarus — are playing down any threat of an imminent attack.

The Wall Street Journal first reported on the contents of the spy chief’s meeting, which marked his first visit to Russia as CIA director. The last trip by the CIA director occurred in late 2021 during President Biden’s term, when spy chief Bill Burns traveled to warn Russian President Vladimir Putin against launching his full-scale invasion against Ukraine. Putin launched the invasion in February 2022.

The Hill reached out to the White House and CIA for comment.

Ratcliffe’s meeting came as Russia has intensified its aerial attacks against Ukraine, with an increasing number of civilians killed. At the same time, Kyiv has seized momentum in the 4 1/2-year war by increasing strikes deep inside Russia and against its military assets in the occupied Crimean peninsula.

The Journal reported earlier that the U.S. intelligence community assessed Putin could try to test the resolve of NATO with a limited assault on an allied country in the next few years. Meanwhile, Russian drone and missile incursions into NATO territory have escalated over the course of the year , while deemed indirect, and are a symptom of its stepped-up attacks against Ukraine.

One European official told The Hill that the U.S. briefed allies about the meeting in Moscow and that it focused on Ukraine. The official added there is no imminent military threat to NATO.

That matched statements coming from Baltic officials, who are stressing the military assessment has not changed. But they pointed out Russia’s hybrid warfare against Europe — a persistent gray-zone campaign — and war against Ukraine are threats to NATO’s security.

“Russia’s threat and possible provocations against NATO must be taken seriously. We remain vigilant, but Estonia’s threat assessment has not changed,” Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna posted on the social platform X.

“The clearer the message to Moscow that NATO is united and our collective defence remains rock-solid, the better. Russia must have no room to miscalculate.”

Latvia’s Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said there are no direct military threats but Russia remains a danger.

“Russia’s aggression in Ukraine and rising hybrid activities against NATO allies leave no room for complacency. Latvia’s threat assessment remains unchanged,” she posted on X .

“Together with our NATO allies, we are taking the necessary measures to strengthen our security.”

Russian Foreign Intelligence Service Director Sergey Naryshkin confirmed that he met with Ratcliffe during the U.S. spy chief’s visit to Moscow, Russian state media reported, and described the meetings as “regular,” citing Trump’s remarks downplaying the extraordinary face-to-face.

Trump, in the Wednesday interview, said the U.S. is trying to end Russia’s war in Ukraine and “something may come out of” Ratcliffe’s meeting. Trump has sought to position the U.S. as a neutral player between Russia and Ukraine, with increased outreach to Putin and downplaying American support for Kyiv.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meeting with Trump last month, pushed for the president to send his top envoys for peace negotiations, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and business partner Steve Witkoff, for a first visit to Kyiv to restart efforts to negotiate with Russia.

Ukraine is also calling for increased supplies of air defenses, in particular U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles, that are the only defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.

articles.title: Malaysian university fires professor who claimed Malays could fly; they taught Romans shipbuilding
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Solehah Yaacob, a former linguistics professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia, went viral last year because of her strange claims, i.
articles.body: Solehah Yaacob, a former linguistics professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia, went viral last year because of her strange claims, including one that said Malays could fly and Malays taught the Chinese the art of "flying kung fu". This was only one of a series of bizarre claims made by her and now the university has distanced itself from her and reportedly fired her.In a statement on Sunday, the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) said Solehah Yaacob, a former linguistics professor, had been terminated from academic service on April 27 and was no longer entitled to claim any affiliation with the institution.The university’s Office for Communication, Advocacy and Promotion said Solehah was now barred from using any official title, position or association with IIUM.“She is no longer a professor nor entitled to claim any association with the university,” it said. “IIUM hopes that this clarification will help avoid any misunderstanding and uphold the integrity and academic standing of the university.”Solehah says her dismissal was unfair, she was an award-winning teacherSolehah is challenging her termination before Malaysia’s Industrial Court and has accused the university of unprofessionalism. She told local news outlet Free Malaysia Today that the Higher Education Ministry had awarded her a Malaysia Research Assessment commendation the day before her dismissal.“I was dismissed within 24 hours and was not allowed to appeal,” she was quoted as saying. “IIUM wanted to pay me the equivalent of six months, but I refused.”Some of Solehah's viral claimsSolehah claimed ancient Romans had learned shipbuilding techniques from Malay seafarers.Another of her claims was that Khadijah, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, had links to the Malay world.Kedah’s iron ore wealth may have originated from meteor showers"She’s clearly gaining significant traction among the Malay community and is now running paid boat-cruise tours that she personally leads. These cruises are specifically designed to demonstrate and validate her research findings by taking passengers to the very locations that support her claims. I’m not joking," James Chin, a scholar of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania, said.While Solehah went viral last year, the speech for which she went viral was from 2022. She defended what she claimed and said she found these things during her extensive PhD research in 2005. articles.title: Meta’s $18bn settlement: How social platforms will change for child users
articles.summary: From night curfew to two-hour limit, Instagram and Facebook will introduce new features for children in the US.
articles.body:
Meta has agreed to a landmark $18bn settlement in a major US federal case accusing it of endangering children, the terms of which will force the social media giant to introduce new safety features to platforms including Instagram and Facebook.

The social media giant has faced an avalanche of legal cases against it this year, mostly arguing that it deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and that they have harmed children. It has already lost two of these and been forced to pay damages.

Under the agreement, child users under the age of 18 will see a slew of changes to their Facebook and Instagram accounts, ranging from night curfews to two-hour usage limits, which Meta must implement as part of the settlement reached on Wednesday with 48 US states.

The agreement could have a global ripple effect as several countries around the world are already taking regulatory action against Meta and other social media companies over their platforms.

So, what is in the settlement Meta has reached in the United States, and how will Instagram and Facebook change for users?

Twenty-nine US states sued Meta, accusing it of designing its platforms in ways that “encourage addictive behaviour, fail to verify users’ ages, encourage adolescents to bypass parental controls, and inadequately safeguard against harmful content and/or intentionally amplify harmful and exploitative content”, according to filings at the Court of Appeal in California.

The first four of the states that originally filed their federal lawsuit against Meta in 2023 – California, Kentucky, Colorado and New Jersey – began their cases in a California federal trial last week.

The attorneys general bringing the case also asked the court to order that changes be made to Meta’s platforms to protect young social media users. In particular, they demanded that Meta introduce a process of parental verification for teenage users; change its “dopamine-manipulating” algorithms; remove image filters for users’ personal images; forbid the creation of multiple accounts; and end “disappearing” messages and posts.

The lawsuit also alleged Meta had violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting, ⁠retaining and using personal data from children under 13 without proper parental consent.

In February this year, Meta lost a multimillion-dollar case brought on similar grounds by a young woman referred to as KGM in Los Angeles, over platform features linked to addiction in younger users.

In March, a US jury ordered Meta to pay $375m for endangering children in a case brought by the state of New Mexico.

Last month, a judge in New Mexico also ordered Facebook and Instagram owner Meta to pay a further $567m in a second phase of the trial .

Meta denied wrongdoing but agreed to settle after evidence was heard that Meta knew its products harmed children’s mental health. The total payout – to be paid over 10 years – is a fraction of Meta’s 2025 revenue of $201bn.

The company, which was originally founded as Facebook in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg, agreed to make maximum payments totalling $16.7bn to 47 US states as well as Washington, DC; Puerto Rico; American Samoa; and the Northern Mariana Islands.

Among those, California could receive a $2.2bn payout, while New York could receive $1.1bn. Texas reached a separate settlement worth more than $1bn. Some states will deposit funds they receive in general accounts, while others will earmark portions to address children’s mental health services.

The settlement does not require Meta to discontinue personalised recommendations or targeted advertising.

It also does not address some content researchers found particularly problematic, including posts that made Instagram users uncomfortable with their body image.

“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” Meta said in a blog post. “We want to get this right for parents and teens.”

What changes will be seen on Instagram and Facebook?

Under the agreement, children under 18 using Meta platforms will be restricted to two hours’ use per day, with a night curfew in place from midnight to 6am. Meta will limit “social comparison” features by hiding likes and reactions to children’s accounts, and will ban “cosmetic procedure filters” that alter the appearance of a user’s image, as a default setting. These settings will only be able to be overruled by parental consent.

The company also agreed to disable the majority of push notifications from the platforms during school hours – 8am to 3pm – for teenage users.

It will also facilitate much closer parental supervision of social media accounts by giving designated adults the ability to more extensively monitor and change settings on a social media account.

Parents and guardians will be able to receive information about time spent on platform apps, and usernames of social connections and accounts sending messages to children.

Supervising parents will also receive daily notifications from Meta any time the teen account messages an adult account for the first time, as well as a link to the adult’s account. Parental accounts will also be notified any time the teen account searches for keywords related to suicide, self-harm or eating disorders.

Meta also agreed to improve the technology used to check children’s ages, using its own as well as third-party tools, with regular outside audits on how well this monitoring is working. This measure is particularly notable because Australia banned under-16s from using social media platforms in December last year. However, the Australian internet watchdog, eSafety, found in August this year that more than eight in 10 young Australian teens and preteens continue to use them – largely because age-check procedures are ineffective.

So far, Meta has only agreed to pay 70 percent of the settlement, or roughly $12.7bn, over the next 10 years. It will only pay the remaining amount, about $5bn, if its rivals – including Snapchat, TikTok and Alphabet-owned YouTube – adopt similar measures and agree to pay the same. It also said it would reduce time restrictions to one hour per day if other platforms do the same.

These changes would be phased over time. Once the court approves the settlement, non-personalised feeds would be introduced within four months; broader compliance measures within six months; and major age-assurance requirements within one year.

While these changes will apply to users in the US, it is unclear if Meta plans to introduce them worldwide. However, Meta is already under rising regulatory pressure in European Union countries and those elsewhere to implement similar changes.

How much difference will these changes make?

Critics and child safety advocates have acknowledged that this settlement has forced landmark changes by Meta, the world’s biggest social media company, which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger, each of which has more than two to three billion monthly active users.

However, critics say the central plank of Meta’s latest settlement deal is the move to restrict teens to two hours per day on platforms, rather than fundamentally changing their addictive algorithms.

Sacha Haworth, executive director of The Tech Oversight Project, which campaigns for youth safety online, said the deal is a “historic settlement that will have a lasting impact, but we cannot truly protect all children and teens until these protections are required on every platform and are permanent – that’s something only Congress can do”.

Ella Bradshaw, policy officer for child safety online at the NSPCC, a UK children’s charity, welcomed moves to rein in “addictive” design features like personalised algorithms and likes. “These are the things that we know keep children hooked and feeling out of control of their screen time, so action here is necessary and welcome. However, important gaps remain,” she told Al Jazeera.

Bradshaw described the settlement as taking “piecemeal action” on tackling risky features and addictive design choices which drive harm of children.

“This means features like disappearing messages, infinite scroll, the ability to gift and livestreaming remain unaddressed. Similarly, little has been announced on how Meta’s AI chatbots will be made safer – better guardrails are needed, particularly when children raise safeguarding concerns.”

Bradshaw also called for stronger protections for younger children as well as protections that “don’t suddenly drop away the moment a teenager turns 18.”

Furthermore, she said: “Not all children have families they can rely on to oversee their online worlds and help them to stay safe. We know that the issue of patchy online protections extends across the online world.

“This settlement must spur governments and regulators to go further faster; taking stronger action across the online ecosystem including private messaging, AI tools and online gaming. Without that wider shift, children will continue to face avoidable harm.”

What action are other countries taking against Meta?

While action against social media giants in the US is mostly taking the form of lawsuits, elsewhere it is regulators who are leading the charge.

In the European Union, regulators are pursuing several legal and regulatory cases against Meta, covering antitrust rules for artificial intelligence (AI) on WhatsApp, as well as child safety protections and addictive platform features under the Digital Services Act (DSA).

The EU specifically accused the group of designing Facebook and Instagram to be “addictive”, adding that Meta has failed to adequately assess the danger its products pose to users’ physical and mental health.

On Thursday, a European Commission spokesperson said it is waiting on Meta to present changes to limit the addictive designs of its social networks.

“We have been very clear … Meta knows what we are expecting from them. … the ball is in Meta’s court,” Thomas Regnier said. “Now it is for the company to offer these commitments in the European Union to protect our kids here, too.”

In June, the UK government also announced a sweeping ban on social media for those below 16 to come into force next year, following a global trend after Australia pioneered it. The UK is also considering overnight curfews and ways to prevent infinite scrolling for those under 18.

In Brazil, a prominent consumer rights organisation, the Collective Defence Institute, filed twin lawsuits for three billion reais ($525m) in damages against the Brazilian subsidiaries of Meta, TikTok and Kwai in October 2024.

Those lawsuits also accuse the groups of failing to implement safeguards against addiction and use by children and adolescents. Since March this year, platforms have been required to link the accounts of children below 16 to legal guardians under Brazil’s Digital Statute for Children and Adolescents.

South Korea’s media regulator also reacted on Thursday to Meta’s settlement, calling for better protections for young users to be ideally applied worldwide, rather than just in specific markets.

articles.title: Kelly Rowland’s Top Self Care Essentials: Olay, JBL, Shani Darden and More
articles.summary: Singer-songwriter Kelly Rowland is the new face of Olay’s Super Collection and a The Voice UK judge. These are her self care essentials at home and in her dressing room.
articles.body: Talking Shop is our series where we talk to interesting people about their most interesting buys. Decades into her career as an award-winning singer, songwriter and actress, Kelly Rowland’s schedule is as packed as ever. She’s a coach on the newest season of The Voice UK; she’s constantly performing across the world (if you caught her on The Boy Is Mine Tour last year, we’re jealous); she’s starring in movies; and she’s spending time in the recording studio (although she can’t tell us exactly why just yet). “I’m really grateful to be doing so many different things that make me smile,” says Rowland, who recently celebrated the 25th anniversary of Destiny Child’s quadruple platinum album, Survivor. One of those things putting a smile on Rowland’s face as of late is her recent partnership with Olay; she’s the face of its Super Collection, which officially comes out today. But her connection to the brand isn’t new. She remembers seeing bottles of Oil of Olay (what Olay was called until the 1990s) on her great aunts’ vanities when she was a child, and watching them apply their creams as a ritual of sorts. “That to me was my first idea of self care,” says Rowland. “The partnership feels like a full circle, cool moment that I’m having with my great aunts.” We caught up with Rowland to learn more about everything she incorporates into her self care routine, especially as she heads into the busy back-to-school season with her kids. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. As a mom to two young sons, Rowland says she’s going into the back-to-school season stocked up on Viva Vitamins’ vitamin C, Gaia Herbs’ elderberry and a generous amount of pocket-sized hand sanitizer. She’s also working on establishing a new routine for her boys. “I want them to come on my runs with me because they’re waking up with all this energy,” Rowland says, noting her go-to running shoes are Hoka or New Balance. “In the mornings, I jog, and then I get on the vibrating plate. I’m trying to make it a fun thing and they’ll feel the benefit of it during the day.” Vibration plates are one of the latest fitness trends that can help your muscles work harder, help your balance and ease stiffness in the body by increasing blood flow, according to experts we spoke to. Many plates, like the LifePro one Rowland uses, come with presets that make using the machine a breeze, even during early weekday mornings. A tour veteran and host of The Voice UK, Rowland says a speaker and fresh mint tea are her pre-show must-haves. “I sometimes make a tea with real pineapple and hibiscus, and it’s so good,” she says. To listen to music in her dressing room, Rowland’s preferred speaker is one from JBL, like this portable bluetooth option that has 28 hours of playing time and crisp, clear sound. Rowland’s wind-down routine is non-negotiable for her own self care. Every night, she uses the sauna in her home and this Shani Darden red light therapy mask to relax. “In the sauna, I sweat everything out; I’m just completely depleted. I drink some water, shower and I get in bed and put my red light mask on and by the time 20 minutes is up, that’s a wrap,” says Rowland. Her FDA-cleared red light mask comes with an optional neck piece, and both parts have built-in LED lights in red, near infrared and blue wavelengths to address signs of aging, acne and pigmentation while boosting collagen, according to the brand. You use the handheld controller to adjust its settings, including the length of your treatment. It’s pricey, but if it helps us get close to skin as flawless as Rowland’s, it may be an investment worth making. Rowland says working with Olay as the face of its Super Collection was a no-brainer both due to her personal connection with the brand and how quickly she fell in love with the new products. The Olay Super Serum, which is infused with activated niacinamide, vitamin C, collagen peptide, vitamin E, and AHA (alpha hydroxy acid), is her favorite. “I’m so used to layering different things on. But I tried this and loved it, especially the glow it gives you,” she says. “[There’s] a little iridescence you get on the cheeks — when we get out in the sun, I like to glisten, I like to glow, and that’s exactly what happens” Rowland adds that paring down her skin care routine has helped save time in her already jam-packed schedule. Why trust NBC Selected? Zoe Malin is a reporter at NBC Selected. She leads the Talking Shop series, interviewing people like Paris Hilton, Maureen Kelly, Lindsay Hubbard and Chase Crawford. Marilyn La Jeunesse is a newsletter editor at NBC Selected. She’s been testing products professionally since 2016 and has previously written for publications like The Cut, Elle, Teen Vogue, Elite Daily, Bustle, and more. To write this article, Malin and La Jeunesse interviewed Kelly Rowaland about her Olay partnership and her favorite products. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Flash flooding underway in the Northeast amid multiple rounds of storms
articles.summary: Rounds of storms are raising the risk of flash flooding in already-soaked parts of the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic on Thursday.
articles.body: Rounds of storms are dumping rain on the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic, raising the risk of flash flooding in the already-soaked regions on Thursday. Flash flooding has been a recurring presence in these regions over the summer: Storms with torrential rain flooded roadways in New York City and New Jersey as recently as last Thursday while also disrupting air travel in the busy corridor. ⛈️☔️In one of the impacted areas? Track the storms, find out your local risk and get more detailed timing from meteorologists in the CNN Weather app⛈️☔️ More of the same is possible into early Friday morning with multiple rounds of storms to come — some of which could be severe with damaging wind gusts and perhaps a tornado. Drenching storms bubbled up late Thursday morning in southeastern Pennsylvania and expended northeast to parts of New Jersey and New York City. Flash flood warnings were active in the region in the afternoon, including in parts of New York City. Another round of storms developed farther west, near the spine of the Appalachian Mountains Thursday afternoon as a cold front started to push into the Northeast from the Ohio Valley. This round has the greatest chance to become severe, especially through the evening. A few storms in Upstate New York and near the West Virginia-Virginia border had already turned severe by mid-afternoon. A Level 2 of 5 risk of severe storms is in place from the New York-Vermont border south into northern Virginia. Washington, DC, Philadelphia and portions of New York City are in this risk area. The strongest storms will lose their punch by midnight, dropping the risk of damaging wind gusts, isolated hail and tornadoes. Even so, rain might not fully come to an end until early Friday morning. Rainfall rates will exceed 1 inch per hour at times Thursday, which could trigger flash flooding, especially in urban areas. A Level 2 of 4 risk of flooding rainfall is in place Thursday from Washington, DC, into parts of southern New York — including New York City — and Connecticut. Most areas will see rainfall totals of around 1 to 2 inches, but some places caught under multiple rounds of the heaviest storms could record as much as 3 to 5 inches of rain. This happened in part of southwestern New Jersey early Thursday afternoon after drenching storms parked over the area and delivered 4 and 6 inches of rain in just a few hours. A new round of showers and thunderstorms could develop farther east on Friday, stretching from southern New England into parts of Delaware and Maryland. These storms aren’t currently forecast to be a significant flood threat, but if they roll over any areas that get soaked on Thursday, that may change.

articles.title: Sophie Brimble's family welcomes review of law after driver deemed unfit to stand trial
articles.summary: The UK government says it is considering changing the law around defendants who are considered unfit to stand trial.
articles.body:
The family of a woman killed after a high-speed race through residential streets says it is a "relief" the government was considering changing the law around defendants who are considered unfit to stand trial.

Sophie Brimble, 20, died after her boyfriend, Jay Bayliss, crashed into a lamp-post in Brynmawr, Blaenau Gwent, in July 2017, while driving at almost three times the speed limit. He was deemed too badly injured for criminal proceedings.

The family launched a petition to give courts greater powers in similar cases, after Bayliss was again declared unfit in 2026 .

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it "agrees the law needs updating and is considering reforms".

The petition, which has been signed by more than 10,000 people, calls for the government to reform the law on unfitness to plead - which is when a criminal defendant cannot stand trial because of their physical or mental condition.

It seeks to end the current situation where, if a jury finds someone caused serious harm or death in a trial of facts, the courts cannot apply "meaningful sanction".

It requests for victim's rights to justice to be considered, and for risks to public safety to be reduced, through increased court powers to apply measures including driving bans.

Aimee Coombes, Brimble's sister, said while her family was relieved by the government's reaction they were "waiting now, and how long is it going to take?"

In 2019 a court found Bayliss' friend Neil Brooks guilty of causing death by dangerous driving, after the two decided to race on a residential road.

Brooks was jailed for eight years and given a nine-year driving ban.

Gwent Police calculated the two cars were travelling at speeds of more than 80mph on 30mph roads in the moments before Bayliss lost control.

Bayliss was subsequently found too badly injured to stand trial, but police reopened the investigation in 2024 after discovering he had successfully reapplied for a driving licence.

He was charged with causing death by dangerous driving, but at the start of the trial in March 2026, the judge ruled, based on medical evidence, that he remained unfit for the criminal process to go ahead.

A trial of facts was then held instead, which means the prosecution set out the case in front of a jury, but Bayliss did not have to play a part in proceedings or be present in court.

A jury found Bayliss responsible for causing Brimble's death by dangerous driving.

But the limited options available to the judge at the sentencing hearing did not include a prison term nor a driving ban, and Bayliss was given an absolute discharge.

This means the court has decided not to impose a punishment because the experience of going to court has been punishment enough.

It also meant the court was powerless to take his driving licence.

"I think we were all a bit shocked with the outcome", said Coombes, from Crickhowell, in Powys.

She said it was at this moment family and friends decided to set up a petition, adding "this needs to change so, no other family has to go through what we've been through".

The Law Commission said the current rules for defining "unfitness" were formulated in 1836, adding they were now outdated and did not take modern medical understandings of capacity into account.

Recommendations it first published a decade ago include a revised test for unfitness to plead, changes to the hearing process and more effective powers for the court where allegations are proved.

"I just want them to sort of stand in our shoes for two minutes to see what we've been through, what other families have been through," said the 32-year-old.

"When we walked out of court, it just felt like Sophie's life didn't matter... she should have had the justice she deserved.

"Knowing that someone else can get that if this all gets changed, that'll be a big achievement."

The MoJ agreed the law needed updating and said it accepted most of the commission's recommendations.

It said it "is considering reforms, including a wider range of court disposals and more effective powers to protect victims and the public", adding this included orders "to strengthen supervision and allow more tailored arrangements to enhance public protection".

The MoJ added that it would also consider how procedures could be made "clearer and more supportive for victims and their families".

articles.title: Burnham’s expected UK ban on Israeli settlement goods draws broad support
articles.summary: A Labour lawmaker tells Al Jazeera sanctions would uphold British morals and legal obligations.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – UK Prime Minister and Labour leader Andy Burnham is expected to soon approve a ban on goods linked to Israeli settlements after the Israeli government issued tenders to build more than 1,200 units for a settlement in the occupied West Bank called E1.

“Sanctions on Israel’s illegal settlements would be a very welcome first step in helping to bring an end to Israel’s unlawful occupation,” Labour lawmaker Richard Burgon told Al Jazeera on Thursday. “The International Court of Justice has been clear that all states have obligations to bring that unlawful situation to an end. These sanctions would be an important move towards meeting our moral as well as our legal obligations.”

The E1 settlement project would ultimately create a continuous Israeli settlement “corridor” between occupied East Jerusalem and the large settlement of Ma’ale Adumim, 7km (4.5 miles) east of Jerusalem. Settlements and outposts on occupied land are illegal under international law.

“The UK government has long-declared E1 to be a red line, and Israel’s total disregard for that red line appears to be what’s motivating these possible actions,” Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel-Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera.

On August 19, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a news release on behalf of the UK government condemning the expansion.

“This Israeli Government’s publication of a tender for the E1 settlement project is an unacceptable and destructive act,” the release read, noting that Miliband had summoned the Israeli charge d’affaires to express opposition to the settlements. “In the coming weeks we will set out a comprehensive set of measures to respond to Israeli government policies, protect the viability of the Palestinian state, target sanctions at those who participate in illegal settlement expansion and support a just and lasting peace for Israelis and Palestinians.”

Last week, Bloomberg News reported that Burnham’s government was “drafting fresh sanctions”.

“We do not comment on speculation,” a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said in a statement to Al Jazeera. “The Foreign Secretary has been clear that illegal settlements threaten the viability of a Palestinian state and undermine security for both Israelis and Palestinians.”

“[Human Rights Watch] welcomes any steps the UK takes towards banning trade with illegal settlements,” Sanbar told Al Jazeera. “We have long been calling on the UK to do more than just condemn. It’s only through concrete action by demonstrating that violations of international law are going to be met with consequences, not just words, that we can expect behaviour to actually change.”

Critics of a ban, most notably the Labour Friends of Israel (LFI), said sanctions could trigger economic blowback for Britons, Palestinians and Israelis or prove to be flat-out impossible.

The LFI’s most recent report noted that Israel’s settlement expansion “weakens the viability of a future Palestinian state and does nothing to enhance Israel’s security”.

Still, the report goes on to condemn sanctions that go “beyond violent extremist settlers and organisations”, noting that such measures would be “impossible” to implement.

For experts, it is unclear where this impossibility lies.

“That’s not true, and that’s not a good enough excuse for the UK to not uphold its obligations under international law,” Sanbar said.

The LFI report further noted that Israel’s settler economy is “inextricably linked” to Palestine’s and Israelis living within Israel’s borders could be “adversely” affected as a ban could become a “de facto boycott of Israel”.

Sanbar said that theory does not add up.

“Opponents of a ban … often try to conflate Israel’s economy with that of the settlements,” Sanbar said. “If business owners move their business out of occupied territory – essentially if they stop violating international law – they can continue their business activities.”

Aside from Israel, the United States has shown a willingness to retaliate against foreign governments protesting against Israel’s actions. The administration of President Donald Trump recently sanctioned several members of the International Criminal Court who have investigated war crimes in Gaza.

The concerns voiced by critics of a ban do not reflect the opinions of the British public.

Recent polling from YouGov suggested that one in two Britons support a ban on trade with illegal settlements and only 16 percent of respondents oppose a ban.

Advocacy organisations like the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) have also noticed a shift from the public.

“May’s local election results and polling from that time has shown that British voters have abandoned Labour in large numbers over its failure to hold Israel to account over the genocide in Gaza,” a PSC spokesperson told Al Jazeera.

More than 140 Labour MPs, Burgon included, have called for the trade ban.

“Burnham is right to plan sanctions on Israeli settlements and ban goods from there,” Labour MP Sarah Champion of Rotherham, who also serves as chairwoman of the International Development Select Committee, said. “The occupation of the West Bank is illegal under international law, and we should not be supporting it in any way.”

Chris Doyle, director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding, wrote to The Sunday Times in support of the ban and in protest against its critics.

“A UK ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories is long overdue,” he wrote, further noting that “this is a problem of Israel’s making.”

Last year alone, Israel allotted more than $800m to expand illegal settlements after Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who is a settler himself, promised in 2023 to “double” the settler population.

The expected UK sanctions, for human rights advocates and experts like Sanbar, mark a welcome step in protesting against Israel’s increasingly brazen campaign against the Palestinians.

“Banning trade with illegal settlements would make war crimes less profitable,” she said.

articles.title: Chinese foreign minister calls for Washington, Beijing to ‘overcome obstacles’ ahead of summit
articles.summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi expressed a commitment to overcoming hurdles in the country’s relationship with the U.S. during a meeting with U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue in Beijing on Wednesday. Their discussion comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s scheduled trip to the U.S. to meet with President Trump next month. While Wang…
articles.body:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi expressed a commitment to overcoming hurdles in the country’s relationship with the U.S. during a meeting with U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue in Beijing on Wednesday.

Their discussion comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s scheduled trip to the U.S. to meet with President Trump next month.

While Wang noted in the exchange that “improving and developing” ties between the two countries under current leadership is critical, he acknowledged the relations “still face various risks and challenges,” according to a readout from the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

“Both sides should put into practice the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, focus on positive agendas, properly manage differences, eliminate interference and overcome obstacles in high-level exchanges between the two countries, and promote China-U.S. relations toward stability, health, and sustainability,” he added, according to the readout.

Perdue called his meetings with Wang and other Chinese officials “productive” in a social media post on Thursday, adding that the two nations were “working together to achieve a constructive relationship of strategic stability with fairness and reciprocity.”

The Chinese leader is scheduled to travel to the White House for a meeting with Trump on Sept. 24. The president last visited Beijing for bilateral meetings with Xi in May.

The upcoming summit in Washington comes amid tensions over the U.S.’s newly announced sanctions against Chinese entities with economic ties to Iran as part of the Trump administration’s “Economic D-Day” campaign against the Middle Eastern country.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian warned Tuesday that these newest penalties would “only further intensify tensions” between the two nations .

“Economic warfare and maximum pressure will not help resolve the issue,” Lin told reporters, according to CNN . “They will only further intensify tensions and conflicts, create spillover risks.”

Additionally, the meeting follows the Justice Department’s Wednesday announcement that it disrupted a multiyear Chinese hacking operation that targeted networks used by NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Senate, the Department of Health and Human Services and other sensitive U.S. government agencies and contractors.

When asked by Fox News about whether the Chinese and U.S. leaders would discuss the hacking scheme during their upcoming summit, Attorney General Todd Blanche said Wednesday that he would not “tell President Trump what he needs to talk to the leadership about in China.”

“This is something that we’ve talked about with our counterparts in China for many, many years,” Blanche continued. “And we know that it’s happening. And they know we know that it’s happening. And it has to stop.”

articles.title: Peter Cullen: Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor dies
articles.summary: Cullen voiced the heroic Optimus Prime in the Transformers TV series and then the Hollywood films.
articles.body:
Actor Peter Cullen, who voiced popular characters including Optimus Prime in Transformers and Eeyore in Disney's Winnie the Pooh franchise, has died at the age of 85.

The Canadian actor began his most famous role - as the heroic deep-voiced Optimus Prime - for the Transformers TV series in 1984, then returned for seven Hollywood films from 2007 to 2023 and other spin-offs.

He voiced depressive donkey Eeyore in TV animation The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh from the late 1980s as well as numerous related shows, films and games.

His other memorable voice parts included KARR, the evil counterpart to KITT in TV show Knight Rider; the clicking vocalisations of The Predator in Arnold Schwarzenegger's 1987 film; and the roars of King Kong in 1976.

He died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles, a statement said.

"Peter Cullen passed away peacefully, surrounded by his loving family - and held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide.

"His family asks that you honour his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember 'be strong enough to be gentle'."

Cullen started his career on Canadian TV and radio and was then a regular on programmes like The Sonny & Cher Show before deciding to concentrate on voice acting.

His Optimus Prime voice was inspired by his older brother, a decorated US Marine and Vietnam War veteran, who suggested he should play the character as "a real hero, don't be a Hollywood hero".

"He said, 'Don't go yelling and screaming. He's strong enough to be gentle.'

"And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime."

Cullen gave his brother a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his death.

The actor's performance as the character earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children's & Family Emmy Awards in 2023.

Cullen's other roles included Monterey Jack in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, and he voiced characters in 1980s and 90s animated series including Spider-Man, Donkey Kong, Alvin & the Chipmunks, Dungeons & Dragons, My Little Pony, Duck Tales and Gummi Bears.

articles.summary: More than 1,300 people are missing — including at least 700 foreigners from two dozen countries — after catastrophic flash flooding hit China and Nepal on Wednesday.
articles.body: More than 1,300 people are missing — including at least 700 foreigners from two dozen countries — after catastrophic flash flooding hit China and Nepal on Wednesday.Scientists are still working to determine exactly what caused the disaster. The US Geological Survey said a glacial collapse — when a large section of ice breaks off a glacier and falls down a slope — and landslide was behind the disaster. Dramatic footage shows a torrent of water hitting the mountainous region, submerging villages and wiping out bridges.The death toll in Nepal has climbed to more than 350 people. Search-and-rescue operations have been hampered by a lack of connectivity, power and resources.

articles.title: Iran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks amid int’l hopes dialogue with US will resume
articles.summary: Officials review efforts being made to reduce war escalation and create ‘appropriate conditions’ for dialogue, Doha says
articles.body:
Qatar’s prime minister has held meetings in the Iranian capital, discussing key issues including the future of the Strait of Hormuz, amid international hopes that dialogue between the United States and Iran on ending the war will resume.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Qatar’s Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani on Thursday discussed a proposed framework that includes the creation of a temporary shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as a possible “joint project” to clear the strait of mines, the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement. Iran says the mines were laid during the war.

The two officials also reviewed “the latest developments in the regional situation … along with the efforts being made to reduce escalation and create appropriate conditions for dialogue, contributing to the enhancement of regional security and stability”, the statement added.

Sheikh Mohammed, who is both prime minister and foreign minister of Qatar, later met separately with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliament speaker and top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Ghalibaf emphasised the need to de-escalate regional tensions, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency. He and Sheikh Mohammed also exchanged views on the current developments in the region and efforts to create suitable conditions for resuming dialogue, the report added.

“Qatar believes that dialogue and diplomatic solutions remain the optimal path for addressing disputes and overcoming crises,” Sheikh Mohammed said in a post on X, adding that his discussions in Tehran serve as “confirmation of our continued efforts to de-escalate tensions … while opening the door to peaceful solutions – including underscoring the importance of respecting freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law.”

Sheikh Mohammed also met with Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezai.

Rezai told him the “US must first take practical steps to fulfil Iran’s conditions and then Iran will proceed to open the Strait of Hormuz”, the Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA) reported.

Rezai also reiterated previous pledges by Tehran that if Washington “starts any evil”, Iran would “bring disaster to its military and economic interests”.

Sheikh Mohammed’s visit follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran involving separate meetings with Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and senior Pakistani officials seeking ways to end the US-Israel war on Iran and reopen the strategic waterway through which about 20 percent of the world’s oil passes in peacetime.

Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, but those deals have since collapsed.

‘Realisation’ that there is room for negotiation

Al Jazeera’s Osama Bin Javaid, reporting from Doha, said that the meeting between Qatari and Iranian officials demonstrated that “there is hope for a deal … [as] it appears that there is now a realisation that there is room for negotiation, mediation and to come back to the table”.

Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu, reporting from Tehran, said that “while there is definitely diplomatic momentum here in Tehran”, it was important to remain cautious as “there is no agreement yet”, with Iranian officials for now only meeting with mediators Pakistan and Qatar.

US President Donald Trump told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that he was “not in a hurry” to resume negotiations with Iran to end the war in the Middle East.

Since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

Iran has for weeks been in talks with Oman to reach the proposed framework and agreement .

Koseoglu said the talks were expected to continue between Iran and Oman and with other Gulf countries.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Wednesday said the two countries had agreed on each country’s share of the waters and any revenues collected from managing the waterway.

Tehran has nonetheless insisted that the strait will not be reopened unless Washington meets its demands, including lifting its naval blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad and removing oil sanctions.

Since the war broke out, Iranian forces have required vessels to obtain permission to transit the waterway and struck ships that failed to comply.

Tehran has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait – a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.
