articles.title: Russian military serviceman killed in St Petersburg car blast
articles.summary: This is the latest in a series of blasts targeting military personnel and others linked to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
articles.body:
A Russian military serviceman has been killed in a “car fire” in St Petersburg, authorities said.

The man was killed, and his wife was injured, when their car exploded in the Pushkinsky suburb on the outskirts of St Petersburg on Thursday, the city’s branch of the Investigative Committee said.

It did not identify the man or give his rank.

The online Fontanka newspaper in Russia’s second-largest city identified the ⁠man as a lieutenant colonel, a 53-year-old high-ranking military officer, and said he died instantly or shortly after the vehicle’s engine started.

Ukrainska Pravda, a Ukrainian news website, claimed that the lieutenant was serving within Russia’s Air Force and Air and Missile Defence units under the Aerospace Forces.

The blast took place at approximately 10am local time (07:00 GMT), according to witnesses, who also added that the explosion completely wrecked the car.

“Currently, investigators and forensic experts, together with operational services, are examining the scene,” the Russian Investigative Committee said on Telegram.

The committee also formally opened a criminal probe, but they initially labelled the incident a vehicle fire rather than officially confirming an explosive device.

Moscow has accused Kyiv of assassination attempts against a number of top Russian military officials amid the Ukraine war. Kyiv has claimed responsibility in some instances, while denying involvement in others.

Al Jazeera correspondent Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said that this latest death is “one in a series of assassinations” of high-ranking Russian military figures.

Ever since Moscow launched its “so-called special military operation in Ukraine in February 2022, Russia has seen a series of high-profile vehicle explosions and targeted assassinations aimed at military commanders and prominent pro-war figures, not just in St Petersburg but also in Moscow,” she said.

On August 5, the director of a factory supplying drones to the Russian military was badly wounded, and his driver was killed, when their car exploded 1,400 kilometres (870 miles) east of Moscow.

Currently, no group has claimed responsibility for this blast, and Ukraine has not commented.

articles.title: Archaeologists are investigating a 400-year-old Polish grave where a young woman was buried in a way meant to prevent her return
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A young woman buried in a Polish cemetery more than four centuries ago was not left to rest in the ordinary way. Archaeologists studying Grave 75 have.
articles.body: A young woman buried in a Polish cemetery more than four centuries ago was not left to rest in the ordinary way. Archaeologists studying Grave 75 have found evidence that her burial was deliberately altered after her death, with an iron sickle placed across her neck and a padlock fastened to her toe. The unusual arrangement appears to have been intended to keep her from leaving the grave or harming the living. Yet the woman’s story is more complicated than the objects suggest.According to Archaeology News Online Magazine, she was probably only 17 or 19 when she died, and traces of expensive silver and gold decoration indicate that she may have come from a relatively prosperous household. Her teeth, bones and DNA are now helping researchers piece together who she was and why someone later feared her return.Young woman in Grave 75 was buried with costly silver and gold decorationThe burial, known as Grave 75, was uncovered during excavations in 2022. Radiocarbon analysis places the woman's death somewhere between 1620 and 1674, when she was probably between 17 and 19 years old.There are signs that she came from a comparatively affluent household. Tiny pieces of material recovered around her head were part of an elaborate textile accessory, made using extremely fine silver and gold-gilded wire. Such decoration would have been expensive, particularly at a time when precious metals were not everyday materials. Her appearance in life can therefore be partly reconstructed from what survived around her. She was young, apparently well dressed and buried with items that suggest a degree of social standing.Woman’s teeth and bones reveal clues about her early lifeReportedly, chemical analysis of her teeth and bones indicates that she consumed relatively little animal protein compared with many other adults buried at the same cemetery. That finding may point towards periods when food was scarce or access to certain foods was limited.It is an unusual combination. Material evidence suggests that the woman had access to expensive clothing or accessories, yet the chemistry of her remains does not suggest a consistently rich diet. Her childhood appears to have been spent locally. Isotope analysis of her teeth points towards the area around Pień, meaning that despite her unusual genetic ancestry, she was probably not someone who had recently arrived from a distant region. DNA provides another piece of the puzzle.DNA testing revealed the woman’s rare maternal lineageGenetic testing placed the woman's maternal lineage in haplogroup J1c2c1. The lineage has Scandinavian roots and is now particularly uncommon among Slavic populations.That does not mean she was necessarily Scandinavian herself. Genetic lineages can persist across generations and move between populations, so a maternal connection to Scandinavia does not establish where the woman or her immediate family came from.The combination is nevertheless interesting: a woman apparently raised near Pień carried a maternal lineage that was unusual for the local population.Her biological history becomes harder to interpret when the evidence from the grave is considered. Something happened after she was initially buried.The grave was reopened before the body had fully decomposedThe position of the bones suggests that the burial was disturbed before the body had completely decomposed. Parts of the skeleton had shifted, while traces of remaining soft tissue indicate that the body was still held together when the grave was reopened.This detail is important because it suggests the unusual arrangement was not part of the original funeral.The later visitors appear to have moved the body before placing the iron sickle across her neck. The blade was turned towards the throat, while the handle had already disappeared. Analysis of the surviving wood identified it as birch.A second object was added at the same time or during the same episode. A padlock was attached to the woman's left big toe. Together, the two objects appear to have served as restraints.The unusual burial reflects fears of a restless or dangerous deadSickles occur in a number of unusual burials from Central and Southeastern Europe. In some cases, they appear to have been placed so that a dead person could not rise from the grave.The arrangement at Pień fits that pattern. The sickle's blade lay across the neck, creating a physical barrier that would have made movement difficult. The lock on the toe offered another symbolic or practical means of preventing the body from leaving its burial place.These actions were tied to beliefs about dangerous or restless dead. In communities where unexplained deaths, illness or repeated misfortune were difficult to understand, suspicion could fall on particular individuals even after they had died.Later descriptions of such practices often use the language of vampires, although people in the 17th century did not necessarily understand the dead in precisely the way the modern word suggests.A burial shaped by fear of the deadThe period in which this woman lived was marked by disease, food shortages and social disruption across parts of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Death could come suddenly, and the reasons behind it were not always clear.That uncertainty could influence how communities dealt with the bodies of people who were regarded with suspicion. A person thought capable of causing harm after death might be buried differently from others, sometimes with objects intended to prevent a return.The sickle and padlock appear to belong to this wider tradition of anti-demonic treatment.The choice of objects may also have carried meanings beyond their physical function. The birch handle, for example, has been linked by the researchers to historical protective associations in the region.Still, there is no evidence that the woman herself had been accused of anything during her lifetime. The archaeological record only shows what was done to her after burial.The green stain remains unexplainedAnother unusual clue was found around the woman's mouth and neck. The bones and surrounding material carried a greenish stain.Chemical examination ruled out the possibility that it came from an old coin placed in the grave. Instead, the colouring appears to have resulted from contact with copper or a copper-rich substance.Exactly what produced the stain remains uncertain. It could have come from an object that has not survived, or from material that was placed near the body during one of the burial episodes. With much of the original grave context disturbed, there is no simple way to establish what happened.The cemetery itself raises questionsThe location of the burial ground adds another layer. Historical maps do not appear to record the cemetery, and archaeologists have not found the crosses or devotional objects that might normally be expected at a Catholic burial site.The cemetery was also situated away from the settlement, close to a crossroads. That location may be significant. Marginal burial places were sometimes used for people whose deaths or reputations made ordinary burial arrangements difficult. It is not possible to say with certainty that everyone buried at the site was feared or rejected, but its setting makes the question worth considering.Grave 75 stands out because the evidence is unusually clear. Someone came back after the young woman had been buried and changed the arrangement of her body.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump coy on ‘economic D-Day’ measures toward Russia, China
articles.summary: President Trump shrugged off questions Thursday about whether countries are taking the U.S.’s “economic D-Day” threats seriously after reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin is set to meet with Iran’s president. When asked if he would punish Putin if the country continues interacting with Iran, Trump said, “it depends.” “I think Russia has behaved quite…
articles.body:
President Trump shrugged off questions Thursday about whether countries are taking the U.S.’s “economic D-Day” threats seriously after reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin is set to meet with Iran’s president.

When asked if he would punish Putin if the country continues interacting with Iran, Trump said, “it depends.”

“I think Russia has behaved quite well having to do with the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.

“For everything they do, we do also,” Trump added. “Somebody said what about China spying. We spy on them too. That’s the way it goes.”

He also shot back at questions on why he won’t sanction Chinese banks that are still doing business with Iran.

“Well, who said I’m not?” he said. “I mean, who said I’m not? You don’t know if I’m doing it. Well, I don’t have to announce everything, do I?”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week warned Iran’s global partners to cut ties or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system, a strategy named Operation Economic Outcast. He wouldn’t name any specific countries and said the U.S. was holding off on immediate action to avoid shaking the global economy.

Bessent said Trump was making calls to world leaders and that officials from the Defense, Treasury and State departments were calling their counterparts to demand action in severing ties with Iran.

Fox News reported Thursday that Bessent will ask his fellow global finance ministers to “sever the economic leakage” of their financial ties to Iran when he attends the Group of 20 summit later this month.

Trump maintained Thursday that boats are traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, adding that he was in no rush to resume negotiations with Iran.

He said Iran is not currently paying its troops and the country is in “deep trouble.”

“We have control, and we have the blockade,” he said. “Iran’s not getting anything.”

articles.title: Mauritania intercepts a migrant boat with 161 aboard, including 17 children
articles.summary: Mauritania said Thursday it intercepted a boat off its coast carrying 161 migrants trying to make their way to Europe.  The country’s coast guard said in a s...
articles.body:
NOUAKCHOTT, Mauritania (AP) — Mauritania said Thursday it intercepted a boat off its coast carrying 161 migrants trying to make their way to Europe.

The country's coast guard said in a statement it "rescued" the migrants off the coast near the fishing village of Amhijrat, north of the capital, Nouakchott.

The boat was carrying people from Senegal, Guinea and Gambia, including 17 children. It had left Gambia's capital Banjul eight days ago and was trying to reach Spain's Canary Islands.

The coast guard said the 161 people are expected to be transferred to a migrant reception center in Nouakchott, Mauritania's capital.

"They were in distress due to a lack of water and food," an immigration official told The Associated Press. "The boat's engine was extremely worn out and exhausted, and the vessel could no longer move forward, it therefore came to a stop at sea."

The official spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

Mauritania's waters have become a major route for people from sub-Saharan Africa seeking a better life in Europe as economic opportunities remain scarce at home.

Last month, the United Nations refugee agency said nearly 150 people died or went missing from boats off Mauritania attempting to go to Europe.

The route toward the Canary Islands is "one of the world's deadliest" with long distances and unseaworthy and overcrowded boats. At least 1,200 migrants died in 2025 along the West Africa-Atlantic route to the Canary Islands, according to the International Organization for Migration's Missing Migrants Project.

articles.title: Lightning strike disrupts flights at Luton Airport
articles.summary: Flights have resumed but the disruption has caused "a number of cancellations and diversions".
articles.body:
A lightning strike on air traffic control systems at Luton Airport has affected flight landings and schedules.

A spokesperson for the airport said operations were suspended between 17:40 and 19:15 BST, "resulting in a number of cancellations and diversions" to about 30 flights.

The disruption had coincided with a "period of severe weather" in the area that had resulted in flash flooding, they added.

The spokesperson apologised to people affected and advised passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.

"Flights to and from London Luton Airport have now resumed following an earlier suspension of operations caused by a lightning strike affecting Air Traffic Control equipment," the spokesperson said.

"The disruption coincided with a period of severe weather across the area, resulting in flash flooding on local roads, and the airport approach.

"As operations return to normal, some flights may continue to experience delays or cancellations as airlines work to recover their schedules."

Gary Nash, from Barton-le-Clay in Bedfordshire, had been due to fly to Spain to attend a family funeral in Alicante on Friday, but his flight was cancelled.

He said he now had to travel up to Birmingham to catch a different flight to get him there on time.

"It's chaotic, absolutely chaotic," he said.

"When you've got 200 or 300 people on different flights that have been cancelled, maybe even more people, 1,000, it's chaotic.

"There's people queuing everywhere and getting nowhere."

Kika Rocha from London had been at Luton Airport ready to travel to Ibiza for a holiday, but her flight was also cancelled.

She described it as a "nightmare" as she initially struggled to get any information.

"At 20:00, the customer service stopped and we were reliant on the people who are at the airport to help us," she said.

"Thankfully we managed to get our flight rebooked for tomorrow, but not to Ibiza.

"We're going somewhere else in Spain and trying to connect, but it's pretty chaotic inside [the airport] at the moment."

Jeff Chan, 26, was due to fly to Venice at 20:50 for a hiking trip in the Dolomites in Italy, but the flight was delayed by three and a half hours.

He received updates through his airline app, but said he "heard nothing from the airport".

"It was actually quite peaceful on the journey here," he said.

"It was only when we got near the airport, it started getting pretty bad."

He added that there was a lot of confusion due to the lack of clarity, with some people expecting to stay at the airport overnight.
